How to watch South Africa vs Bangladesh 2026 2nd Test: Free Streams & Preview
Temba Bavuma's absence shouldn't stop South Africa's Test juggernaut
After winning the first Test rather comfortably, South Africa – the world's No. 1 Test side and now at the top of the World Test Championship (WTC) standings – will look to continue their dominance in the second South Africa vs Bangladesh Test at SuperSport Park, Centurion.
Read on as we explain how to watch the South Africa vs Bangladesh 2026 2nd Test online, on TV and potentially for free wherever you are in the world.
Watch South Africa vs Bangladesh 2nd Test 2026 for free
Yes. South African viewers can stream the 2nd Test between South Africa and Bangladesh live for free on SABC 3 and via the SABC+ streaming service.
This will also be the case for England's tour next month, so now is a great time to start catching a big summer of cricket in South Africa.
Outside of South Africa today? You'll need NordVPN to watch your regular streams as normal and avoid getting geo-blocked.
How to watch any South Africa vs Bangladesh 2026 2nd Test stream using a VPN

🇺🇸 How to watch South Africa vs Bangladesh 2026 2nd Test live streams in the US
Willow TV is the place to watch the 2nd Test between South Africa and Bangladesh in the US.
Willow TV is available via cable or as part off Sling TV's Desi Binge Plus or Dakshin Flex plans – starting from $10 per month.
Visiting the US from South Africa? Use NordVPN to watch your free home coverage.
🇬🇧 How to watch South Africa vs Bangladesh 2026 2nd Test live streams in the UK
UK viewers can watch the South Africa vs Bangladesh 2026 2nd Test live on Sky Sports.

Visiting the UK from South Africa? Use NordVPN to access your preferred coverage of the South Africa vs Bangladesh 2nd Test.

Outside India? Get yourself a VPN and watch your home coverage of South Africa vs Bangladesh.

South African resident in Australia? Get yourself a VPN to stream the Test match for free.

A DStv access package is the best way to stream the action, with prices starting at Rs399/month.
SABC is free and will have live coverage every day on SABC 3.
Abroad right now? Just use a VPN and tell your device that you're back home. Then you'll be good to go.
South Africa vs Bangladesh 2026 2nd Test FAQs
South Africa vs Bangladesh 2nd Test Preview
The 1st Test looked closely contested for the opening few days. Bangladesh started well, scoring 400 in their first innings, with centuries from Towhid Hridoy and wicketkeeper Litton Das. The Proteas, however, responded with a massive 557, taking a 157-run lead. A maiden Test century from opener Marques Ackerman, another hundred from Ryan Rickelton, and Kagiso Rabada's career-best 72 at No. 10 helped the hosts turn things around.
For a moment, it looked like the match could be heading for a draw. But Simon Harmer ripped through Bangladesh's batting order on the final morning, picking up six wickets as the visitors were bowled out for just 168. Kagiso Rabada also chipped in with three wickets in the second innings to finish with eight for the match and earn Player of the Match honours. South Africa then needed just 12 runs to seal a nine-wicket victory.
The Proteas will now be without captain Temba Bavuma for the 2nd Test. He has been ruled out after sustaining a right calf strain while batting in the first innings. Tony de Zorzi is expected to come in as his replacement at No. 4, while Aiden Markram is likely to lead the side.
While Bangladesh have never won a Test against South Africa, their first-innings performance will give them some confidence. They showed they can score big runs even in challenging overseas conditions, with Hridoy, Litton and Tanzid Hasan all making valuable contributions.
However, captain Najmul Hossain Shanto admitted that missed chances and too many no-balls cost his side dearly. If Bangladesh can address those issues and avoid another batting collapse, they could make life difficult for the hosts and potentially pull off an upset, just as they did against Australia earlier this year.
What are the South Africa vs Bangladesh 2026 2nd Test squads?
South Africa: Aiden Markram (c), Marques Ackerman, Matthew Breetzke, Corbin Bosch, Tony de Zorzi, Simon Harmer, Zubayr Hamza, Marco Jansen, Senuran Muthusamy, Keshav Maharaj, Mulder, Anrich Nortje, Dane Paterson, Kagiso Rabada, Ryan Rickelton
Bangladesh: Najmul Hossain Shanto (c), Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Tanzid Hasan, Mohammad Naim, Mominul Haque, Mushfiqur Rahim, Litton Das (wk), Towhid Hridoy, Jaker Ali, Taijul Islam, Taskin Ahmed, Hasan Mahmud, Shoriful Islam, Ebadot Hossain, Khaled Ahmed, Mahfijul Islam
What is the South Africa vs Bangladesh Test series schedule?
- First Test, Johannesburg, The Wanderers Stadium (15-19 November) - South Africa won by 9 wckts
- Second Test, Centurion, SuperSport Park (23-27 November)

articles.title: Amazon's Black Friday sale is live for Australia: I'm hunting the top deals on Day 7 — these are my picks for the 70+ best discounts
articles.text:
Amazon's Black Friday sale is live for Australia: I'm hunting the top deals on Day 7 — these are my picks for the 70+ best discounts
There are some all-time low prices on coffee machines, air fryers, vacuums, headphones and more
Amazon Ausralia's Black Friday sale for 2026 is in full swing, having kicked off when the clock struck midnight on November 17. The biggest sale of the year will continue through to Cyber Monday on November 30, giving you 14 days of deals mayhem.
Amazon Australia has gone big already, with all-time low prices on hero items including the Sony WH-CH730N headphones, Ninja Slushi and Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow, to name a few.
• Shop all Amazon Black Friday deals
I'll be adding deals to this page throughout the sale, so make sure to keep checking back for the latest drops. If you've never tried Amazon Prime before, you can sign up now and get yourself a free 30-day free trial that you can cancel any time if you don't want to pay the ongoing AU$12.99 subscription fee.
Amazon quick links
• Amazon Bestsellers: see what everyone else is buying
• Lightning deals: hurry — just hours to buy limited stocks
• Deals ending at midnight: you don't want to sleep on these
• Amazon devices: up to 70% off Kindles, Echos, Ring, Eero & more
• Electronics bestsellers: USB cables, chargers, batteries & more
• Computing bestsellers: discounts on cables to peripherals
• Appliance bestsellers: from the humble kettle to room heaters & more
Editor's picks: today's top deals
This USB-C charger is extremely compact, which makes it an ideal choice to leave in a bag as a backup option. It can fast charge most phones and with 20V output, even top up a laptop if needed.
We may not have tested these buds ourselves here at TechRadar, but it’s hard to ignore the 100K customer reviews on Amazon. While often discounted to this price, if you’re after dependable Bluetooth buds on a budget, these are a great option.
The MacBook Neo hasn't seen much in the way of discounts yet (in fact, it has had a price rise), so this meagre 5% off is the best we have seen. Still, it's something at least, and it's well worth checking out our MacBook Neo review for the full scoop.
Boasting a 12,000dpi 'Hero' sensor, as well as 6 programmable buttons, a 250-hour battery and onboard memory for your settings, the Logitech G305 Lightspeed Wireless Gaming Mouse is ideal for competitive play. Want to know more? Check out our review, but not that only the blue and lilac colourways get the best discount.
While they don't include ANC, these affordable Sony headphones are still a solid buy, plus this is the best price we have seen on Amazon so far. In our Sony WH-CH530 review we said that "they supply great sound for the price, with beautiful warm bass, clean mids, and expressive treble."
This little pod machine is very popular among TechRadar's Aussie team. We've had past and present staff say how much they love it, and they'd even buy it at full price. With a very compact footprint and plenty of Vertuo pods to choose from, you'll get delicious coffee at just the press of a button.
If you're after a compact model that can feed one or two people, this Philips option is great for under a hundred dollary-doos. It's been hovering around the AU$95 mark for a while, so it's quite the best deal, but it's still a discount that's hard to pass up on an air fryer with a staggering 13 preset cooking options.
This discount matches the Blink Video Doorbell System’s last all-time low price during the last Prime Day sale in July. It’s worth noting, though, that many of the features are locked behind the AU$4.95/m Blink Basic or AU$15/m Blink Plus subscription plans, so those costs should be considered if you want video storage, person detection and more. Amazon is also offering a bundle with two Blink Mini 2K+ cameras for AU$54.98 or 71% off, perfect for a good starter home security system.
Already quite affordable, this Blink video doorbell can rival anything from the more expensive Ring line, while also offering a long battery life and IP65 weatherproofing. Also included is the Sync Module that you'll need to make everything work, but you will need to take into account that it requires a Blink Subscription Plan if you want all its functions at your fingertips.
If you're after a really good electric toothbrush that won't cost an arm and a leg (or some teeth), then this is it. It's an entry-level oscillating brush, which means it rotates at fast speeds and may not be ideal for people with sensitive or bleeding gums as that movement can be harsh, but it sure does remove a heck of a lot of plaque and keeps your teeth healthy.
If you don't enjoy flossing the traditional way, use the power of water instead. Removing plaque using three different water pressure settings, this handy flosser will clean out those hard-to-reach gaps that your toothbrush can't. Plus, it's cordless, meaning you can take it on your travels too. Admittedly these were a lot cheaper in July (just over AU$48), but it was bestseller then, so it would be remiss of me to not include it here again.
The Lavazza Jolie machines are excellent and affordable alternatives to Nespresso. This Evo model just has a single button for extracting coffee (compared to the Jolie Plus that has programmable buttons), making it oh so simple to use.
This food processor's biggest drawcard is its small footprint (30cm tall and 16cm wide), making it great for those with smaller kitchens, but it also has a powerful 650W motor to help blitz foods to slice, grate, chop and knead in seconds. This is the lowest price we've seen for the MultiPro Go, and you can read the full review here.
We might be in the middle of winter, but there's no denying some parts of Australia need a good fan year round. This Vornado model creates tornado-like air flow that circulates around the room. Note that this is the smallest model in the range, ideal for bedrooms.
Amazon devices
Amazon's current midrange 7-inch Kindle has dropped to cost less than its newer 6-inch sibling in this Black Friday deal, making it the best choice if you want to pick up one of Amazon's e-readers on the cheap. That said, with more storage than the standard model, a brighter screen and wireless charging, the Paperwhite Signature Edition is arguably better value than the base model above if you think you'll make full use of the storage and its wireless charging capabilities. It's currently down to AU$257, or 36% off.
The Kindle Colorsoft is one of the best ereaders with a colour display, even offering a feature to make the hues more vivid. While I wouldn't recommend at full price, this discount makes it a little easier on the pocket for the 32GB version that also has wireless charging.
Kindles are known for their reading capabilities, but with the Kindle Scribe, you get that and a whole lot more. With a wide range of writing features, you can take notes, create sketches and brainstorm like a pro. I love its 10.2-inch glare-free screen with an ambient light sensor, and it's battery life is excellent too. It's now the previous-gen model, but arguably better value than the 2025 3rd-gen release.
Amazon's Echo Dot it's a great smart speaker with decent sound and Alexa built-in. It also has motion detection and can measure temperature, which is handy if you have a connected thermostat. It is a little long in the tooth now, having released in 2022, but it's a bargain at this price.
The Echo Dot Max features almost 3x the bass of the Echo Dot (5th gen), and its sound can automatically adapt to your space, making it the perfect addition to any smart home or party setup. We gave it a nice 4 stars in our review, namely for its great smart home capabilities and stellar sound. Now at its lowest-ever price.
Launched in October, the latest Echo home display devices have gotten a much-needed glow-up Echo Show 8 and the Echo Show 11. Aside from the updated in-cell touch and negative liquid crystal screens, both devices include new front-facing stereo speakers and a custom woofer for room-filling spatial audio. The key difference between the two? The Echo Show 8 has a smaller 8.7-inch display.
With all the same great features as the new Echo Show 8 above, if you're after a larger home display screen to connect to your Ring devices, check recipes while cooking or control your smart devices using Alexa, then the 11-inch Echo Show could be the move for you. Also discounted by 35%.
Headphones & Audio
These affordable earbuds with ANC are brimming with features, including a range of ANC modes, EQ presets and other audio adjustments. They sound good (but you'll want to tweak it from the default) and they'll last up to 7.5 hours with ANC on before they need a recharge. Check out our Earfun Air Pro 4 review for more info and take advantage of this offer.
The JBL Grip plugs the gap between the smaller Clip and formidable Flip. It's a compact speaker that delivers a big sound, offers impressive protection against dust and water and has some nifty LED lighting on its rear.
If you're looking for a great set of noise-cancelling over-ears but don't want to pay a lot of cash, this deal on the excellent WH-CH730N headphones is worth a look. As we said in our WH-CH730N review, they offer great value-for-money option with an excellent set of features, solid sound quality, and a nifty, foldable design,
The Beats Pill is a sturdy, classy portable speaker that you can use anywhere from the living room to the poolside, thanks to its IP67 waterproof and dustproof rating. It also has a substantial 24-hour battery life, so you can listen for a long time without worrying about recharging. This matches the last all-time low from February 2026.
Offering “incredible sound” according to our review, the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds have all the power and quality you’d expect from a Bose-branded item while providing the benefits of an open-ear form factor. The Immersive sound is excellent, and they give up to 7 hours of music. While they have been slightly cheaper, this is the not far off the best price we have seen since lately.
If you're finding yourself a bit baffled by Bose's huge range of QuietComfort headphones, we don't blame you. This SC variant gets you the audio brand's current mainstream (and well-regarded) noise-cancelling over-ears with a soft carry case – thus the 'SC' – rather than the hard case the regular version comes with. The cans themselves are identical. We haven't reviewed this pair but they are a modest update on the four-star QuietComfort 45, which we praised for superb noise-cancelling and, OK battery life and decent sound.
We gave these stunning earbuds 4.5 stars in our review as they have class-leading audio handling and impeccable sound quality that rivals the best wireless earbuds. With balanced sound, effective ANC and a great battery life, these Sennheiser buds will make any audiophile smile.
Dropping to the the lowest price we've seen, this is a fine chance to snap up Apple's flagship earbuds. The ANC is best-in-class, and the sound and fit have been improved over the Pro 2. Check out our review for the full story.
Now down to AU$797 in all colours, there's never been a better time to secure Apple's ridiculously good noise cancelling over ears. While the design hasn't changed much, the internals have been upgraded to deliver even better ANC performance, Lossless audio over USB-C and a wealth of useful features made possible by the new H2 chip.
There's much to be said still of wired headphones, as they offer a more reliable and stronger connection to your source devices. You will likely need a 3.5mm-to-USB or -Lightning adapter (or one of the best headphone DACs) to get them connected to your phone, but do so and you’ll be rewarded with a gorgeous, high-fidelity sound. And, being Sennheiser, they’re impeccably built and are super comfortable to wear for longer sessions.
The JBL Charge 5 can bring the party, and quite loudly I might add. I use this Bluetooth speaker at home myself and love it, with up to 20 hours of playback. It's also dust and waterproof (IP67 rating), so you can take anywhere, plus it will double as a phone charger in a pinch if you need some extra juice on your handset.
We haven’t reviewed this Bose soundbar, but if it’s anything like the brand’s other models, we’re confident it will do a mighty fine job of boosting the sound from your TV, ideal when watching movies. If you want to add even more low-end grunt, it works with the company’s Bass Modules (sold separately). A Dialogue mode helps to boost vocals, and if you fancy a dance around your bedroom or living room, Bluetooth is onboard for you to stream your favourite tunes.
Coffee machines
This do-it-all machine from Ninja really can make pretty much any coffee you could want, whether it be hot or iced. It will select the right grind size, has user profiles to store settings, and even two bean hoppers so you can swap out for different beans.
Also available in stainless steel for the same AU$948 price.
The best entry-level bean-to-cup coffee maker has received a good discount for Black Friday, although not quite as good as the AU$359 we saw during Prime Day. It's simple to use, taking care of the grinding, tamping and pouring for you. The porta filter will even automatically slide into position for you. Do note there's no milk frothing here, but a matching milk frother is available.
This compact manual coffee machine can pour up to two espresso shots at once and features a steam wand for cafe-quality milk foaming. There's no built-in grinder, but you either use ground coffee beans or invest in a separate grinder using the cash you save with this deal.
If you've already got a decent coffee maker but one without a grinder, just add this Breville machine to get fresh ground coffee. It has over 60 settings for precise control over your beans, meaning you should be able to extract the most delicious shot from the grind catering to your taste.
A welcome saving on Breville's answer to the SodaStream. Not only can you use the InFizz Fusion to carbonate water, but you can fizz any liquid you can think of — other than hot beverages of course. This nifty machine is sure to be a hit during at-home cocktail nights.
The Breville Bambino Plus is incredibly simple to use, and can take care of most of the coffee making process for you. Grind some beans into the porta filter, insert it into the group head and use the one-touch controls to brew. It also has a hands-free milk texturing system for expertly frothed milk, while ThermoJet technology means the machine is ready to use in seconds. There's very little you need to do to simply enjoy the results — now AU$20 more than what it cost at the start of the sale.
With a nice saving, it's hard to dismiss this Breville coffee machine deal. The Barista Express has a built-in grinder, tamper, and bean hopper, so there's no need to buy a separate grinder or hand tamp. Available in a few colourways under the same listing, only the Charcoal model gets the full discount.
We've only reviewed the more expensive Touch model, but if you take your coffee seriously – and want a barista-level cup of joe easily, this is the deal for you. Offering automatic grinding, dosing, tamping and milk texturing, this machine lets you go from beans to latte in seconds.
Vacuum cleaners
This affordable Dreame stick vac can handle regular everyday cleaning tasks — it may not be the most powerful tool in the shed, but it sure will keep it clean. Even handy for the boat, the car or your home for not a lot of cash.
Now down by a huge AU$660, Dyson's Detect Submarine houses a powerful suction and a superb runtime of up to 60 minutes. It can handle all floor types, including wet and dry messes.
We haven't tested this cordless vacuum ourselves but user reviews are glowing and I think that says something. For quick and daily vacuuming. This one always proves popular during major sales, and I reckon it will be once more, as this is a new all-time low price in Australia.
This Shark cordless vac is on the more simple side of things, but it gets the job done with powerful, dynamic suction, that adjusts depending on the floor type you're cleaning.
In our Ecovacs Deebot X8 Pro Omni review, in which it scored an impressive 4.5-star score, we called it a "chatty all-in-one robot vacuum that cleans better than most others". Its biggest drawback is its regular price, but this deal takes care of that — letting you enjoy its strong suction, efficient edge cleaning, effective mopping and smart navigation.
A huge discount on what is a relatively new flagship model from Ecovacs. We haven't tested this version out yet, but if it works as well as the previous X8 Pro Omni did, then I think this is a good premium robovac to consider without the hefty price tag.
Kitchen Appliances
The Nutribullet is great value if you need a powerful blender for your liquid breakfast needs. In fact, it will even come in handy if you want to use it as a regular blender to make sauces, dips and small batches of soup. This model has a 900W motor and comes with a single 700ml cup.
The Ninja Slushi lets you skip the ice and still enjoy perfectly smooth icy drinks with very little effort. Whether you're craving a frappe, smoothie, or even a cheeky spiked slushi, its multiple drink modes have you covered. Even better, the current deal price is near to the lowest we have seen on Amazon. Check out our Ninja Slushi review for the full rundown.
This compact air fryer packs 1700W of power into a portable design, with two borosilicate glass containers that serve as both frying baskets and serving dishes. The borosilicate glass can withstand extreme temperatures, making it easy to take your favourite foods from frozen to crispy, and it's safer to use than any non-stick basket. The Crispi also comes with two removable crisping grates and two snap-on container lids for easy storage.
It's got a cult-like following and two members of our own staff are massive fans. If you love your chilled desserts — ice creams, gelatos, smoothies — but want to control your calorie intake, you really should consider getting the Ninja Creami. This Deluxe edition gets you three containers, which is great value at this price.
Not a big discount and even I balk at recommending a toaster that costs more then AU$50, but I have the Black Truffle model of this 2-slice toaster and trust me when I say it's one of the best toasters I've used. Sure, it's overkill for the average person but if you can get the perfect toast every morning (or arvo or evening), I think it's worth considering.
This Shark fan has twisting ends that allow it to shoot air out in any direction. The blades can be positioned horizontally or vertically too, and while the ends need manual intervention, all other controls can be adjusted via a remote control.
PC & Gaming
A 100Hz-refresh-rate monitor for just AU$100? Sign me up! This display from Lenovo may be a bit small at under 24 inches with a 1080p resolution, but it uses IPS technology for sharp image quality. This is price is the lowest we've seen this monitor go on Amazon.
This handheld gaming PC has been cheaper before, dropping to the AU$899 mark but, then again, nothing really comes cheap these days. Importantly, though, this is a great performer, with a vivid 8-inch display and 144Hz refresh rate for smooth gameplay. It's also rather nice looking and comfortable in the hand.
Phones, tablets & wearables
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 Wayfarer Smart Glasses are a great choice for anyone who likes wearing sunglasses but wants the perks of an AI-powered wearable. Just like wireless earbuds, you can listen to music and talk on the phone, but you can also take POV photos and videos in 3K.
A small but welcome discount on the Google Pixel Watch 5. This competent wearable delivers accurate GPS, all the essential health and fitness tracking features you need, and an attractive design. If you're upgrading from a Pixel Watch 3 or 4, you won't notice a huge leap, but for everyone else, it's easily the best Android smartwatch right now.
It looks like an iPhone and can rival Apple's performance too, thanks to a powerful chipset under the hood. In fact, our tester was quite impressed with this phone in our Xiaomi 17T review, with the biggest issue being bloatware. If that doesn't bother you, we gave this one four stars.
Samsung's answer to the AirTag, the SmartTag 2 works with select Samsung phones to help you find mislaid items. It has a built-in hole for easier attachments, up to 700 days of battery life and it's water-resistant.
The Vivoactive 5 contains a lot of the premium Garmin features found in its more expensive offerings, while also priced closer to conventional smartwatches. These features include on-board GPS, on-device storage for offline music via Spotify, and fitness metrics like Body Battery and VO2 Max.
This watch received a perfect 5 stars in our Amazfit Active 2 review, and the fact that it only costs AU$159.19 is gobsmacking considering its feature set. The closest Garmin alternative, the five-year-old Forerunner 55, still retails for AU$349 and is much more limited in comparison.
We called this the best smart ring for battery life (rated up to 12 days + a further 150 days with the charging case) while also being a more affordable option than Oura and Samsung at full price. The Gen 2 added a sleep apnoea tracker to make up for the price hike over its predecessor. Again, be sure to source the sizing kit first as not all smart rings are made the same.
Cameras
Dropping to the best prices I've seen, this fun little camera might well be worthwhile for a budding content creator. While PowerShot V10 struggles a little in low light, it's a great little companion to keep with you when you're out and about or want to use it as a webcam or streaming camera. It even has its own little stand for that.
Beauty & grooming
If you didn't know what a 'sonic' brush is, it's quieter and gentler than an oscillating electric toothbrush (like Oral-B). The DiamondClean 9000 has 4 cleaning modes, and one of them gets you 3 intensities. This value pack gets you a his-and-hers version, plus the glass is actually the charger.
Offering one of the most fuss-free shaves, the Philips OneBlade 360 is a nigh-on essential tool for any man's grooming routine. The cutting blade itself can move in any direction, ensuring constant, comfortable contact with your face to remove your beard entirely, while an included guard comb allows you to trim your facial fuzz to a desired length.
The Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra is a solid choice if you want one device for general trimming and getting a closer shave. It includes interchangeable SkinSafe trimmer and foil heads, a built-in LED light and a waterproof design for wet or dry use, while USB-C charging and the included travel case make it easier to take on the road.
Gaming
All the regular Assassin's Creed goodness you love, no in feudal Japan! Become both a lethal assassin and powerful samurai in this open world that allows you to switch seamlessly between the two.
Enter the wizarding world of Harry Potter, in Lego form on the Switch 2, with this collection of two games, covering Lego Harry Potter: Years 1-4 and Years 5-7.
It's fair to say Wolverine received a mixed reaction from gamers when it launched. If you were initially hesitant to play as the clawed mutant, then perhaps this 45% discount at Amazon could be enough to persuade you.
"It isn’t cheap, but the audio quality is near perfect". That was us reviewing the Inzone H9 II, and while it's still a premium price, this is a big discount on a superb gaming headset.
This deal offers you a decent saving on Meta's best 'affordable' headset, and a close second to its best ever headset according to our resident VR headset tester. In fact, he thinks it's the second-best headset anyone can buy from any brand, and it's only a more tempting offer thanks to this limited-time deal, which includes a free copy of GOLF+ to get you started.
Are you a Prime member yet?
If there's one thing you need to do to take full advantage of any major Amazon sale is to become a Prime member. While I think many Aussies already are, some of you might still be wondering what it means to be a Prime member, what you're actually paying for and if shelling out a monthly or annual sum is actually worth it.
In short, if you're a regular Amazon shopper, I think it's worth signing up for it. Your AU$9.99 monthly fee (or AU$79 annually) gets you free and expedited shipping on thousands of eligible products without needing to fulfil a minimum spend.
That fee also gets you free access to Prime Video (which does have some excellent shows and movies), along with Prime Reading and Prime Gaming. Just the first one more than makes up for the investment you're making in my opinion.
While there are generally no Prime-exclusive deals right now, there are the occasional coupons or lightning deals that won't explicitly say it's for Prime members, but will only appear if you're signed in with a paid account. You can find out more about the subscription service in my dedicated guide to what is Amazon Prime in Australia.
It's also worth noting that if you've never tried this service before, signing up now will get you a 30-day free trial that more than covers the sale. If you don't want to pay at all, you can cancel as soon as the sale finishes. Keep in mind that if you use the same email later to sign up again, you will not get that free trial later even if you didn't use all 30 days.

articles.title: A 12,000-pound AI construction loader pops wheelies and spins autonomously
articles.text:
Monster Truck or Killdozer: Researchers used Machine Learning to teach a 12,000-lbs John Deere skid-steer loader to do 'complex acrobatic manoeuvres' i.e., street dancing
AI taught a 12,000-pound loader to pull off two-wheel stunts
- A John Deere loader now balances on two wheels without an operator.
- Researchers trained the construction machine in simulation before real-world demonstrations.
- The loader can spin while maintaining balance on uneven terrain.
A 12,000-pound John Deere construction loader has learned to perform movements normally associated with stunt driving, using artificial intelligence rather than human operators.
Researchers affiliated with ETH Zurich, Blue River Technology, Gravis Robotics and Intel used reinforcement learning and computer simulation to teach a John Deere skid-steer loader to perform autonomous acrobatic manoeuvres previously associated with highly skilled human operators.
They trained the machine to lift itself onto two wheels, maintain balance, navigate uneven surfaces, and execute controlled spins without assistance.
AI turns construction equipment into an autonomous stunt performer
The John Deere 332G skid-steer loader is an industrial machine designed primarily for moving materials and performing construction work.
Instead of relying on conventional programming, researchers developed an artificial intelligence system that learned suitable movements through repeated training and feedback.
The training process relied on reinforcement learning, a machine learning approach in which an artificial agent improves its decisions through rewards and penalties.
They first trained the control system inside a simulated environment before transferring its learned instructions to the physical construction machine.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
This approach addressed several difficulties associated with automating heavy equipment, particularly machines controlled through complicated hydraulic mechanisms.
Hydraulic systems introduce nonlinear responses, fluid movements, flexible components, and operational delays that make precise automated control considerably more difficult.
The machine's considerable weight also makes physical experimentation dangerous, particularly when testing movements that require lifting its entire body.
Computer simulations allowed researchers to develop and refine control strategies before attempting the same operations using actual construction equipment.
Once transferred, the trained system enabled the John Deere 332G to raise itself onto two wheels without assistance from an operator.
It could subsequently maintain that position while traveling across rough ground and following predetermined movement patterns.
The five-ton loader can balance, spin, and manipulate its bucket
The demonstrations extended beyond balancing, with the autonomous machine performing controlled rotations while maintaining its unusual two-wheel position.
The research team also trained it to move its front bucket repeatedly while balancing, before returning safely onto all four wheels.
These movements require coordinated control of the loader's wheels, hydraulic equipment, and center of gravity during continuous changes in mechanical stability.
The system must therefore adjust its movements while accounting for the machine's changing physical condition and surrounding terrain.
Overall, the study examines how reinforcement learning and simulation-to-reality transfer can automate heavy equipment performing movements.
The findings could have practical implications for construction, mining, and material-handling industries, where automated machinery must operate under demanding physical conditions.
However, the experiments focused on specialized demonstrations rather than establishing that conventional construction operations can already run without human supervision.
For now, the ability to perform such stunts shows how machine learning can control heavy equipment beyond its conventional operating movements.
Whether similar systems can deliver dependable performance during everyday industrial work will require further testing under ordinary operating conditions.

articles.title: So much for green AI: Harvard report exposes the fossil fuel reality behind the US AI boom
articles.text:
Hyperscaler data centers are now using as much energy as entire US states — and the problem is only going to get worse
Just 403 US data centers are burning more power than Michigan
- Report claims 403 hyperscale facilities in the US consume as much power as Michigan
- Their CO2 emissions reportedly exceed Denmark's entire annual greenhouse gas output
- Fossil fuels still supply more than half their electricity requirements
Electricity consumption from large data centers in the United States has reached levels comparable to those of entire states, new research has claimed.
A report from Harvard assessed 403 hyperscale facilities, and found that their combined annual power requirements rival electricity consumption of the entire state of Michigan.
The associated carbon emissions also exceeded Denmark's annual greenhouse gas output, raising questions about the environmental costs of expanding digital infrastructure.
Hundreds of facilities account for enormous electricity consumption
The researchers examined electricity consumption between May 2024 and April 2025, estimating that the facilities required between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours annually.
The combined consumption represented approximately 1.8% of total American electricity demand during the period.
The assessment also attributed approximately 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions to these facilities, indicating considerable environmental consequences.
This latest estimated electricity consumption is at least two to three times higher than comparable estimates in 2018.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Fossil fuels supplied approximately 54% of the electricity consumed by the facilities, with natural gas accounting for 30% and coal contributing another 15%.
This dependence becomes particularly significant because many installations operate in regions where coal remains an important electricity generation source.
Four states accounted for more than half of the electricity consumption examined in the research.
Virginia, Ohio, Oregon, and Iowa collectively hosted a substantial concentration of these energy-intensive computing installations.
Expanding AI infrastructure could increase electricity demand
Even though this report is alarming, the authors warn that the research captures only the early stages of the industry's expansion.
“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard, wrote in a press release.
“The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”
The assessment also excludes facilities whose electricity comes from dedicated, off-grid gas generation, leaving additional consumption outside its calculations.
Current general estimates claim that the U.S. has about 5,000 data centers with no less than 1,500 under construction.
This growing demand has attracted political opposition, with Republican Senator Josh Hawley calling for a temporary suspension of new data center construction.
Democratic lawmakers have also pressed developers to accept greater responsibility for the infrastructure and environmental consequences associated with their operations.
Meanwhile, Senators Shelley Moore Capito, Mike Lee, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Martin Heinrich have pursued legislation intended to accelerate infrastructure permitting.
Their proposal would also require developers to contribute more toward the electricity costs associated with their facilities.
The debate now involves more than accommodating expanding computing capacity, particularly as artificial intelligence development increases pressure on existing electricity infrastructure.
Public opposition has also grown, with several surveys indicating widespread concerns about the construction of new data centers.
Much of the resistance centers on electricity consumption, water requirements, and noise pollution, with countries such as Thailand introducing noise limits for data center operations.
Some companies are consequently turning to existing buildings, including former indoor marijuana farms, for conversion into data center facilities.
However, these conversions carry their own challenges, as computing operations may require more electricity and water than the previous agricultural activities, while noise pollution remains an unresolved concern.

articles.title: AI-Assisted Cyberattacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks and Fintech Firms
articles.text:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has warned that threat actors are carrying out artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyber attacks targeting information and communication technology (ICT) assets in the country.
This unsanctioned activity has resulted in unauthorized financial transactions at banking and financial services entities, as well as technology service providers supporting government-linked payments and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts.
"In the observed incidents, attackers targeted business records and approval processes to carry out unauthorized transactions through otherwise legitimate systems," CERT-In said in an advisory last week.
The incidents have been found to include the following methods -
- Abuse of business applications and service provider-operated workflows, as opposed to direct exploitation of payment-related APIs.
- Modification of business records or approval relationships, followed by the use of legitimate payment processes.
- Use of trusted systems and established approval procedures to process unauthorized transactions without raising any alert.
- Exploitation of security blind spots in independent verification, reconciliation, and review of changes to business records..
CERT-In did not reveal how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom. The activity has not been attributed to any specific threat actor.
The agency also said that separate threat-hunting has uncovered the use of AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks (AOFS) across enterprise, technology, government, academic, and research sectors to conduct the following actions -
- Automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems, services, and potential attack paths.
- Rapid generation and modification of exploits for known vulnerabilities, including by analyzing software patches and related technical information.
- Using a cluster of AI agents to undertake intrusion tasks, such as reconnaissance and privilege discovery, in parallel.
- Modifying scripts, requests, and attack methods in response to errors, blocked attempts, or information returned by targeted systems.
- Using valid credentials, legitimate administrative functions, trust relationships, and external infrastructure to burrow deeper into target networks.
"Organizations should review the security of business applications, critical records, user identities and third-party interfaces," CERT-In said. "Existing monitoring and incident-response arrangements should also account for the risks arising from misuse of trusted business processes and automated intrusion activity."
The development comes as Indian entities have witnessed a spate of AI-assisted cyber attacks on financial entities, even as it disclosed that AI agents under research and evaluation "exceeded their task authorization and made unauthorized access" to ICT assets.
"In the financially motivated campaign against Indian entities, agentic tooling compressed the time between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours," CERT-In said. "In addition, the campaign highlighted that multi-agent operations run in parallel for hours to days to achieve the attacker goals, consistent with the documented multi-agent capability of these tools."
Earlier this month, the agency also warned that a threat group named Crafty Falcon is behind a wave of AI-driven attacks on financial firms and has used offensive penetration testing tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN, and CyberStrikeAI to automate the intrusions at machine speed.
According to the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the attacks have targeted banks, non-banking financial companies, and fintech companies, leading to multi-crore (equivalent to 10 million) unauthorized transactions through fund disbursement systems and APIs.
"Perpetrators exploit unpatched software or misconfigured internet-exposed servers / IT systems to compromise the infrastructure," I4C said. "Hackers then target automated fund disbursement systems or special interfaces (APIs) used for payments and fund transfers. The money is sent to 'mule' accounts (accounts used by criminals) across different banks and then quickly moved or withdrawn through IMPS/NEFT."
India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, has also alerted of rising cyber attacks on financial infrastructure, urging banks to provide details of their ability to stay ahead of AI-related threats, Reuters reported late last month.
The Surge in AI Attacks
The advisories also come at a time when organizations around the world are being targeted using AI tools, giving attackers a way to "execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity." Last week, the European Commission confirmed that attackers armed with ARTEX broke into its HR, medical reimbursement, and translation systems. The first signs of the attack were detected on October 22, 2026.
ARTEX has also been implicated in a recent supply chain attack on IT management software company ConnectWise and Barracuda, with the latter revealing that a financially motivated criminal weaponized an exposed valid cloud access key provided to a third-party vendor to map its reach, repurpose discovered secrets to access more systems and look for seed phrases, and exfiltrate more credentials and secrets.
"In all, the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts in roughly 44 hours [between November 1 and 2]. The work was methodical and tireless," Barracuda said. "The probe names, the other indicators we collected, the order in which the attacker worked through our systems, and its built-in routines for hunting credentials and wallets all match ARTEX."
Frameworks like ARTEX manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute, and adapt tactics across multiple kill chain stages, including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance, lateral movement, and data exfiltration.
They can translate tactical goals described in natural language into machine commands that are executed by specialized AI agents. It integrates with various external LLMs, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, SpaceXAI Grok, Zhipu GLM, and Kimi.
"ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an alert this month.
"The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale."
Check Point, in a report published this month, said it uncovered more than 1,800 publicly exposed instances for ARTEX, with attackers leveraging the tool to conduct opportunistic, financially-motivated cybercrime.
"Analysis of agent conversations revealed that these systems work almost fully autonomously, once the initial goal is set: most actors barely interacted with their agent fleets and mostly asked for progress or directed the agents to a new target," the company said.
Data security firm Cohesity said threat actors using ARTEX are gaining access to systems that receive less security attention, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales support applications, legacy services, third-party integrations, and applications built by individual business units.
"In a research network we operate, a threat actor linked to Rhysida used an AI framework to rewrite tools in response to obstacles, often within minutes, and more than 150 versions of a single script reached a domain controller within a day," it said.
In a report published last week, Google's Mandiant and Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) identified what it described as the first observed instance of attackers using an autonomous AI framework with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.
The AI framework, called "exploit_agent," integrates with multiple frontier and local large language models (LLMs). It's designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention. The attacker, suspected to be Russian-speaking, is said to have leveraged the framework to target French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector.
"The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software," Mandiant and GTIG said. "It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention."
Some of the other notable incidents where AI agents and models do the legwork are listed below -
- Use of CAIRN in intrusion activity against targets, including in the aerospace sector in the U.S.
- Embedding LLMs into influence operation workflows to produce synthetic media, create convincing virtual personas, and generate and publish content.
- Use of Google's Gemini API, along with tools from multiple AI providers, to build an end-to-end influence-as-a-service (SaaS) platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, specifically across Europe and the Middle East.
- Use of LLMs by a China-linked contractor called Leaky Castle to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data
- Abuse of a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure by a China-nexus threat actor to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents.
- Use of LLMs by North Korean threat actors to generate resumes and prepare for job interviews at Western organizations.
- Creation of fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms by a suspected North Korean hacking group called Midnight Neptune (previously UNC1069) in attacks aimed at cryptocurrency entities in North America and Europe using job- and ClickFix-themed lures. These personas have been found to direct targets to fraudulent meeting platforms, which are used to run diagnostic fix scripts via ClickFix. "Following initial compromise, the actor pivoted into internal code repositories to execute a supply chain vector internal to the organization: modifying .claude/settings.json configuration files so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor," Google said.
- Use of CyberStrikeAI ("43.240.29[.]11") between September 30 and October 16, 2026, to validate stolen AWS credentials, harvest secrets from Secrets Manager, pull EC2 user data, decrypt an SSM parameter, and send a remote command. "The audit log does not show what the command was or whether it succeeded," Elastic Security Labs said.
- Use of Hermes, in combination with DeepSeek, by a threat actor called Silent Lynx in cyber espionage operations targeting Central Asian governments and critical infrastructure from April to October 2026 to assist with reconnaissance, data collection, and erasing traces of activity from compromised systems.
- Use of ARTEX to exploit a vulnerable custom PHP upload function and stage a web shell, and use it to access secrets and API keys, and ultimately compromise a company's development pipeline to alter a Git repository and deploy an attacker-controlled Kubernetes pod.
- Use of an AI coding assistant to revive a stalled attack at a U.S. retail organization and come up with ways to bypass defenses and steal credentials after their commands were blocked by security software in late September 2026. The attack is assessed to be financially motivated, based on the threat actor's scans for passwords in point-of-sale scripts and an IP address overlap with a prior campaign targeting online retailers.
- Use of CAIRN by a Chinese-speaking attacker between August and September 2026 and pairing it with GLM and DeepSeek models to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attacks, attributed to CL-STA-1238, have targeted advanced semiconductor manufacturing, U.S. defense policy, and civil society sectors, achieving unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the entities, including valid credentials, personal data, military and government identities, and the creation of persistent administrator accounts in a production system. "Cairn coordinates its activities through a shared 'blackboard," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Agents read the blackboard and write their findings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject 'hints' at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Confirmed findings accumulate as immutable facts, and the agent queues its next actions as intents."
- Use of ARTEX to gain access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. "Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure," Cloudflare said. "LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments."
- Use of ARTEX to generate deepfake videos to trick identity verification checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges and steal AI credentials at "industrial scale" to gain free access to models. Amazon has characterized the second campaign as a "self-sustaining operation in which stolen keys paid for the LLM inference powering further credential hunting." Targets include LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders such as Dify, FastGPT, Langflow (CVE-2025-3248), RAGFlow (CVE-2026-28797), Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama.
- Use of CAIRN by a suspected Chinese-nexus threat actor to discover a zero-day vulnerability (GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94) in MONAI Label, a medical imaging application, and use it to gain complete control of a server within 11 minutes. The activity was detected in September 2026.
"An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert," CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said in a report shared with The Hacker News.
"The most extensive operation targeted a Redis (remote dictionary server) instance at one university that was configured to allow access without authentication. The agents worked through a long list of known techniques for taking control of an open Redis server. The agents that failed against the hardened Redis target ran continuously for 16 hours without breaks, sleep, or working-hour constraints."
What's notable about accelerating AI-enabled attacks is that the technology is not just used as a force multiplier but has also emerged as the target.
"The integration of AI-enabled tools into enterprise workflows is creating new attack surfaces, particularly where those tools hold privileged access to code, credentials, data, or connected applications," Recorded Future said. "Developer tools are a primary target of attacks on AI systems. Threat actors exploited weak access controls and software supply-chain vulnerabilities to steal data or establish persistence."
Besides automating the time-consuming phases of intrusions, LLM-driven pentesting frameworks also lower the technical barrier to entry, enabling actors with minimal expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks.
"Now, an attacker can give an agent a goal in plain language," GitGuardian said. "The agent can investigate the environment, select tools, execute commands, interpret the results, and decide what to try next. The tools are also becoming better at recovering from failed attempts. An agent can encounter an error, interpret the response, modify its next command, and continue investigating."
"Anyone with access to AntiFox or ARTEX can just verbally say into the dictation, 'find exposed credentials, determine what they access, and identify valuable resources.' That incantation initiates a series of technical actions that previously required considerably more hands-on expertise."

articles.title: Cómo revisar si tu router tiene la última actualización y cerrar el acceso remoto
articles.text:
Actualizar el firmware, el programa interno que hace funcionar el router, y desactivar la administración remota son los dos ajustes que más reducen el riesgo de que un equipo doméstico sea infectado. La recomendación se repite en las guías de la agencia de ciberseguridad de Estados Unidos (CISA) y cobra actualidad tras un ataque a routers de la marca GL.iNet.
El 20 de noviembre, GL.iNet informó en un aviso de seguridad que una persona no autorizada aprovechó una falla en sus servicios de administración remota en la nube para instalar software malicioso en algunos routers y dispositivos KVM, que permiten controlar una computadora a distancia.
Ahora bien, la empresa dijo que cerró esa vía de ataque, pero que esa medida no elimina el programa de los equipos ya infectados.
BleepingComputer, que analizó el código malicioso, informó que la empresa no precisó cuántos clientes resultaron afectados. La consultora RemoteToHome, que administra routers de esa marca, dijo que halló actividad sospechosa en 152 de los 183 equipos que revisó. Los investigadores advirtieron que parte de esos hallazgos puede no estar ligada al ataque de noviembre.
La guía vale para cualquier marca. Los nombres de los menús cambian según el fabricante, por lo que CISA aconseja consultar el manual del equipo o al proveedor de internet.
Primero, actualizar el firmware
Los routers, a diferencia de un teléfono, no siempre se actualizan solos. El Centro de Ciberseguridad y Comunicaciones de Nueva Jersey (NJCCIC) explica que ese sistema interno suele descargarse e instalarse de forma manual. CISA indica entrar en la página del fabricante, comprobar cuál es la versión más reciente para el modelo y compararla con la instalada.
Para ver la versión instalada, se abre el panel de administración desde el navegador. La dirección y las credenciales de fábrica suelen figurar en una etiqueta pegada al equipo, según CISA. Allí, en el apartado de sistema o de actualizaciones, se instala el archivo del fabricante. Si existe la opción de actualizaciones automáticas, CISA recomienda activarla.
En el caso de GL.iNet, la empresa informó que programó para el 22 de noviembre un firmware estable con correcciones de seguridad para routers y KVM. Recomienda instalarlo aunque la revisión no detecte infección. Los modelos KVM tienen desde ya una versión de prueba (beta) con esas correcciones.
Cerrar las puertas que no se usan
El segundo ajuste es la administración remota. CISA explica que esa función permite entrar a la configuración del router por internet y que desactivarla impide que alguien haga cambios sin conectarse antes a la red, ya sea por cable o por Wi-Fi. En el panel suele aparecer como administración remota, acceso desde internet o acceso por la nube.
Tercero, cambiar el usuario y la clave de administrador. CISA señala que las credenciales de fábrica pueden estar disponibles en internet. Pide una contraseña larga, aleatoria y distinta de las demás. La clave del Wi-Fi es otra: CISA sugiere una frase de cinco a siete palabras sin relación entre sí y de al menos 16 caracteres.
Cuarto, revisar el cifrado de la red inalámbrica. CISA considera seguros WPA3 Personal o WPA2 con AES. Si el router solo ofrece WEP, WPA o WPA2 con TKIP, aconseja pedir un reemplazo al proveedor de internet o comprar otro equipo.
Quinto, apagar las funciones que se usan poco. CISA recomienda desactivar WPS, el botón o código que simplifica la conexión de dispositivos, y UPnP, que permite a los aparatos del hogar abrirse camino por la red.
La agencia advierte que UPnP puede servir para propagar software malicioso. También sugiere crear una red de invitados para los dispositivos domésticos que solo necesitan internet.
Si el router es de GL.iNet, hay una revisión adicional
GL.iNet indica buscar el texto exacto crond -i /tmp/.log entre los procesos en ejecución. En un router, se entra al panel de administración, a Sistema, Configuración avanzada, y se inicia sesión en LuCI, la interfaz avanzada. Allí se abre Estado, Procesos, y se busca “tmp/.log”. También se puede usar SSH con el comando ps | grep tmp.
Si aparece ese texto, la empresa pide tratar el equipo como infectado. Para los KVM, ofrece instalar la versión beta o restaurar los valores de fábrica, lo que borra la configuración. GL.iNet dice que, si la revisión no encuentra el indicador y no hay otros motivos de sospecha, no hace falta restaurar el equipo. Para consultas, ofrece el correo support@gl-inet.com.
La revisión de la empresa tiene límites. Usuarios del foro de GL.iNet advirtieron, según BleepingComputer, que las instrucciones pueden no detectar equipos con otras puertas traseras. La empresa dijo que seguía investigando el alcance y que avisará por correo a los clientes que identifique como afectados.

articles.title: Nomadic raises $6 million to deploy autonomous drones
articles.text:
These 4kg drones land on live 420 kV power lines to recharge from the magnetic field — logging 20,000 hours hunting hidden bottlenecks across European and US grids
Nomadic drones land on live power lines to recharge and spot issues on the line
- Nomadic drones recharge directly from magnetic fields surrounding energized power lines
- Each 4 kg drone can monitor approximately 25 kilometers of transmission infrastructure
- Nomadic reports more than 20,000 operating hours across three countries
Electricity networks are facing mounting pressure as renewable energy projects, factories, and data centers demand connections faster than infrastructure expansion can accommodate.
However, identifying weaknesses along existing transmission routes remains difficult because conventional monitoring systems cannot easily capture changing conditions across every section.
A Munich technology company called Nomadic has developed autonomous drones that attach themselves to energized power cables and collect measurements without interrupting electricity transmission.
Drones monitor power lines while harvesting energy from magnetic fields
Each Nomad aircraft weighs approximately 4kg and can attach itself to an energized conductor, drawing operating power through electromagnetic induction.
This arrangement eliminates the need for frequent battery replacements or separate charging infrastructure while allowing continuous observation of electrical transmission conditions.
The aircraft can reach deployment locations within minutes, avoiding the extensive preparation and temporary shutdowns traditionally associated with installing equipment directly onto operational cables.
Nomadic reports accumulate more than 20,000 operating hours across electricity networks in Germany, Norway, and the United States.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Its systems have operated at voltages reaching 420 kV, representing the upper range commonly encountered across European transmission infrastructure.
Testing has also covered temperatures reaching -25 degrees Celsius, with the company reporting reliable operation using energy harvested directly from surrounding electromagnetic fields.
Each aircraft can monitor approximately 25 kilometers of transmission infrastructure, compared with stationary monitoring equipment generally installed at intervals between one and five kilometers.
This coverage allows operators to obtain information across longer distances without deploying numerous permanently mounted monitoring devices.
The company uses its software. Nomadic OS software to analyze measurements collected by its drones alongside weather conditions, grid models, and historical line data.
With this information, operators can identify sections developing faults and those with limited transmission capacity.
“Grid operators often have a good picture of what happens at each substation. Everything in between, along kilometers of line, has been much harder to see, because installing anything on a live line is very difficult,” said Andreas Moldskred, CEO and co-founder of Nomadic.
$6 million in funding will support expansion and remote drone relocation
Nomadic has secured $6 million in seed financing led by Foundamental, alongside Verve Ventures, Cyan Ventures, existing backers Outlander VC and Asia2G Capital, and individual investors.
The company intends to increase deployments with electricity providers throughout Europe and the United States while expanding its workforce.
Another priority involves introducing remote relocation capabilities for commercial customers next year.
This feature will allow operators to direct drones remotely between different power line sections without physically retrieving and redeploying them.
Chief Technology Officer Lauritz Weil said developing equipment capable of attaching itself to energized conductors required extensive engineering and testing.
“Landing on a line carrying up to 420 kV, in wind and at minus 25 degrees, and then running on power from the magnetic field around it, is a hard robotics problem,” Weil said.

articles.title: El chip cuántico Willow de Google superó en un juego el límite de las computadoras tradicionales
articles.text:
El procesador cuántico Willow, de Google, ganó un juego matemático de coordinación en el 98,3% de las partidas, por encima del 88,9% que alcanza como máximo cualquier estrategia clásica. El resultado se publicó en la revista Science y no significa que exista una computadora cuántica comercial.
El experimento fue realizado por Google Quantum AI y colaboradores. Según el resumen del estudio, el equipo usó un procesador de qubits superconductores (las unidades básicas de información de una computadora cuántica) para demostrar que un fenómeno llamado contextualidad cuántica permite superar límites clásicos en ciertas tareas.
La contextualidad cuántica significa que el resultado de una medición no está fijado de antemano, sino que depende de qué otras cosas se miden al mismo tiempo. Los investigadores, citados por el medio especializado Decrypt, lo explicaron así: no se pueden asignar valores fijos y preexistentes a todo lo que se podría medir.
Un juego de cuadrícula con cuatro qubits
La primera prueba fue el juego del cuadrado mágico de Mermin-Peres. Dos jugadores, sin comunicarse, deben completar partes de una cuadrícula de tres por tres con respuestas que cumplan reglas de filas y columnas y coincidan en la casilla compartida.
Una estrategia clásica pactada de antemano acierta como máximo en ocho de cada nueve asignaciones, es decir, el 88,9%. Con qubits entrelazados, la teoría indica que se podría ganar siempre. Willow ganó el 98,3% de unas 900.000 pruebas, según Decrypt, y el ruido inevitable del equipo impidió llegar al ideal.
Google también midió el grado de contextualidad con una prueba matemática. Cualquier modelo con resultados predeterminados obtiene como máximo 4 puntos, mientras que la teoría cuántica permite hasta 6. Willow registró 5.590, con una incertidumbre de 0,008, según el mismo medio.
De 71 a 105 qubits, con límites
El estudio incluyó otras dos tareas con más qubits. En un juego de paridad en el que hasta 71 qubits entrelazados debían dar respuestas coordinadas, Google se mantuvo por encima del límite clásico, que tiende a 50% a medida que suben los jugadores. Los autores también verificaron entrelazamiento genuino en 45 qubits.
La segunda tarea, un problema de función lineal oculta, usó 105 qubits en un circuito poco profundo, es decir, con pocos pasos de cálculo. El procesador logró cerca de 60% de éxito. Decrypt precisa que esa prueba se compara con un límite clásico conjeturado, no demostrado, y que su instancia más grande falló en cuatro de cada 10 ejecuciones.
Por eso el avance se lee como una prueba de calidad del hardware y no como una ventaja práctica. El propio resumen del estudio dice que el trabajo introduce una forma de evaluar procesadores cuánticos con algoritmos basados en contextualidad, y que mejora el estado del arte en fidelidad y tamaño del sistema en dos de las tareas.
Lo que el resultado no demuestra
Decrypt señala que el 98,3% corresponde a cuatro qubits y que la prueba de 105 qubits mide un desafío distinto y más acotado. Tampoco se trata de computación tolerante a fallos, la que corrige sus propios errores y sería necesaria para tareas de uso general.
El mismo medio recuerda que la amenaza futura a las firmas digitales de Bitcoin depende de una computadora cuántica capaz de corregir errores, algo que, según su análisis, está lejos de ocurrir. La tarea de 105 qubits fue un circuito matemático sencillo, no un ataque criptográfico.
El estudio apareció en el volumen 394, número 6826, de Science, entre las páginas 870 y 874, y su versión completa está disponible en la web de la revista.

articles.title: OpenRouter Drops 3 Providers After Researchers Catch Months of Prompt Theft at AI Hosting Firms
articles.text:
Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week.
Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored.
OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said.
The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said.
The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it.
The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack.
The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls.
One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server.
On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections.
"A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer.
The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found.
The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys.
One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt.
A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab.
A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint.
Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.
The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt.
In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings.
OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned.
The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties.
The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week.
Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers.
Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted.
What the Providers Have Disclosed
An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections.
Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated.
A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window.
At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July.
The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts.
Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers.
Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three.
The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week.
What Users Should Do
The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price.
Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check.
Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys.
A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.
