articles.title: Kann es einen „Ideen-Detektor“ geben? Ein neues Tool soll das für Forschungsarbeiten prüfen
articles.text:
Mensch oder ChatGPT: Neuer KI-Detektor soll erkennen, woher die Idee für einen Text kommt
Schulen, Hochschulen, Wissenschaft und Medien, sie alle befinden sich in einem Katz-und-Maus-Spiel mit künstlicher Intelligenz: Welche Hausaufgaben, Studien und Berichte stammen von einem Menschen und welche wurden von einem großen Sprachmodell verfasst? Wo wurde KI als Hilfsmittel verwendet, um Texte zu formulieren und wo war sie womöglich stärker involviert, vielleicht sogar beim Erstellen von Daten oder gar der Ideenfindung?
Während sich der Wissenschaftsbetrieb langsam damit arrangiert, dass Paper zunehmend mithilfe von KI verfasst werden, bleibt die Antwort auf die Frage nach dem Ursprung von Ideen schwierig. Texte lassen sich, mal mehr, mal weniger zuverlässig, auf KI-Formulierungen hin untersuchen. Doch kann es auch einen „Ideen-Detektor“ geben?
Forschungsidee: Was stammt vom KI-Modell und was hat sich ein Mensch überlegt?
Ja, sagen Forschende der Universität von Maryland und Google Deepmind. In einem noch nicht von unabhängigen Expertinnen und Experten geprüften Preprint stellen sie Idea Lens vor: Einen Algorithmus, der mutmaßlich erkennen kann, ob die Ideen eines Textes – und nicht nur der Text selbst – von einem Menschen oder einer Maschine stammen.
Während Prosa-Detektoren wie Pangram einen Text auf oberflächliche Merkmale wie die Auswahl der Wörter, die Satzstruktur und statistische Textmuster hin untersucht, prüft Idea Lens den Text auf seine argumentative und inhaltliche Struktur. Denn auch darin lassen sich Hinweise drauf finden, ob ein Sprachmodell zum Einsatz kam.
Idea Lens zerlegt Texte in ihre diskursive Struktur
Das Tool, das auf einer Website selbst ausprobiert werden kann, funktioniert so: Idea Lens zerlegt einen Text, etwa eine wissenschaftliche Studie, zunächst in seine Einzelteile. Für jedes Segment wird sowohl der Inhalt als auch die Funktion beschrieben: Handelt es sich bei der Passage um einen Beweis, um eine Empfehlung oder eine Beschreibung, um nur drei mögliche Funktionen zu nennen. Um die Prosa als Störfaktor auszuschließen, zum Beispiel charakteristische Formulierungen eines Autors, wird der Inhalt durch ein eigenes Sprachmodell umgeschrieben; der ursprüngliche Schreibstil und die Wortwahl verschwinden nahezu komplett. Ein netter Nebeneffekt dieser Paraphrasierung: Das Modell kann mit vielen unterschiedlichen Sprachen arbeiten.
Am Ende entsteht eine diskursive Struktur, die jedem Text innewohnt, ganz gleich ob kurze eine E-Mail oder ein 1.000-Seiten-Roman: Autorinnen und Autoren entscheiden, wie sie Inhalt und Funktion anordnen. Ein großes Sprachmodell tut das ebenfalls – nutzt dafür aber immer ähnliche Muster. Genau diese soll Idea Lens erkennen, indem es die Abfolge und Art der Argumente bewertet.
Testdatensatz stammt aus einer Zeit vor und nach ChatGPT
Damit es valide Aussagen treffen kann, musste Idea Lens natürlich seinerseits zunächst trainiert werden. Dazu haben die Forschenden das Modell mit rund 800.000 Texten aus verschiedenen Quellen gefüttert, die mithilfe des KI-Detektors Pangram als entweder KI-generiert oder von einem Menschen geschrieben gelabelt wurden. Dass die Analysen von Pangram nicht 100-prozentig perfekt sind, sieht das Team als Vorteil, um ein gewisses „Rauschen“ in die Trainingsdaten zu bekommen.
Getestet wurde Idea Lens schließlich an einem Korpus von Texten, von denen ein Teil aus der Zeit vor ChatGPT stammt und man relativ sicher sein kann, dass sie nicht mithilfe von KI geschrieben wurden. Gegenüber Pangram überzeugte Idea Lens vor allem bei gemischter Urheberschaft, zum einen bei Texten, die von einer KI (mit)geschrieben wurden, aber auf menschlichen Ideen beruhen: Wo herkömmliche Detektoren wie Pangram 4 dieselben Texte bis zu 92,4 Prozent als KI-generiert einstuften, sank die Rate bei Idea Lens, abhängig von der diskursiven Struktur des jeweiligen Textes, auf bis zu 7 Prozent. Soll heißen: Das Modell konnte an dem Testdatensatz, von dem die Forscher:innen wussten, ob die Ideen mit oder ohne ChatGPT entstanden waren, deutlich zuverlässiger den Menschen oder die Maschine als Urheber ermitteln – ein wichtiger Aspekt bei der Bewertung von wissenschaftlichen Studien.
Im zweiten Fall, nämlich bei Texten, die Menschen auf Basis einer KI-generierten Struktur verfassen, erkannte Idea Leans die KI-Herkunft in 68 Prozent der Fälle. Prosa-Detektoren kamen hier auf eine Trefferquote von unter 10 Prozent.
Der Mensch wird präzise, die KI bleibt vage
Interessant ist, welche Unterschiede Idea Lens in der diskursiven Struktur in den Texten von Mensch und Maschine fand. Demnach enthalten menschliche Texte mehr spezielle Details oder Handlungsanweisungen, welche die Kernaussage oder die Schlussfolgerung des Autors oder der Autorin unterstützen. Eine KI formuliert dagegen universeller mit austauschbaren Details. Auch benennen Menschen eher Grenzen und Hürden, während die KI Nachteile und Zielkonflikte eher unter den Tisch fallen lässt oder unterschätzt.
Trotz des innovativen Ansatzes, habe Idea Lens noch einige Schwächen, sagen unabhängige Forschende. So sei das System nicht für das immer häufiger auftretende Szenario der „Co-Autorschaft“ geeignet, bei dem Mensch und Maschine schon den Ideenprozess gemeinsam gestalten und es keine klare Unterscheidung mehr gibt. Außerdem bliebe unklar, welche Hinweise das Modell genau heranzieht und wie gewichtet, um seine Aussagen zu treffen – auf diesen Black-Box-Charakter weist das Team um Rishanth Rajendhran auch selbst hin.
Wie Rajendhran gegenüber Science sagt, sollte Idea Lens zusammen mit anderen Erkennungsinstrumenten eingesetzt werden, um den Einsatz von KI im gesamten Werk eines Forschers oder einer Forscherin zu untersuchen, und nicht nur in Einzelfällen. „Angesichts des Reputationsschadens, den solche Vorfälle mit sich bringen, ist es wichtig, dass wir vorsichtig damit umgehen“, sagt er. Die Forschenden sehen den Einsatz des Modells letztlich nicht nur darin, um Menschen der Nutzung von KI zu überführen. Sondern auch darin, dass sich Wissenschaftler und Wissenschaftlerinnen selbst bewusst machen können, welche Rolle KI in ihrer Arbeit spielt.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 16.11.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: Ukraine revives its grounded fleet of 500+ US-made Puma drones with homegrown anti-jamming tech — anti-jamming upgrade triples range to 31 miles
articles.text:
Ukraine revives its grounded fleet of 500+ US-made Puma drones with homegrown anti-jamming tech — anti-jamming upgrade triples range to 31 miles
The battlefield continues to evolve.
The U.S. delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions. These hand-launched uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) are equipped with optical and infrared sensors for surveying the battlefield, but the evolving electromagnetic warfare landscape meant that the entire fleet had to be grounded. Now, Ukrainian defense firm Rise Technologies has upgraded the drones with its Palych communications system, which allows the UAVs to withstand the advanced electronic warfare (EW) environment found on the frontlines in 2026. According to United24 Media, this new component allows drone operators to select the drone’s operating frequency band to avoid heavily jammed channels and maintain communications during flight. It also increases the range of the Puma to 31 miles (50 kilometers) from its basic range of 10 miles (16 kilometers).
Russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs. Because of this, we’ve seen various innovations to counter the countermeasures, like the use of fiber optic drones, which are essentially jam-proof, and the installation of a camera and magnetic compass on Russian drones to counter GPS jamming. Ukraine has also devised a "flying modem" relay system for its drones, allowing its forces to conduct strategic drone strikes even without the use of finicky Starlink connections. The indigenous communications system was also installed on other drones from DJI and Autel, as well as on some attack UAVs, giving Ukrainian drone operators an advantage on the battlefield.
The proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them. The U.S. has already deployed high-energy lasers to shoot down Mexican cartel drones crossing its southern border, while the Royal Navy is testing the DragonFire laser that can target UAVs traveling at up to 400 mph while only costing $13 per shot. Israel has also deployed its 100,000-watt Iron Beam system, while China has built a man-portable anti-drone laser system that weighs 55 pounds and can hit targets up to 1,600 feet away.
These laser systems are ideal for taking down a few drone units. But for drone swarm threats, microwave systems are a better solution, as they could take down multiple drones in a single shot. Some examples of this include the Leonidas AGV from the U.S. and Turkey’s Aselsan Ejderha, or “Dragon” in English, which uses high-power electromagnetic systems to overwhelm the sensitive electronics found inside most drones.

articles.title: El gran centro de IA de Huawei visto por satélite: China tiene energía, pero aún le faltan chips
articles.text:
Huawei está montando uno de los mayores centros de datos de China en Horinger, en la región autónoma de Mongolia Interior. Lo sabemos porque la propia Huawei lo anunció y también porque lo hemos visto desde el cielo gracias a los satélites Copernicus Sentinel de la UE y el estadounidense Vantor. Y como dice el refrán, una imagen vale más que mil palabras. Y si es a alta resolución, más todavía.
A vista de pájaro pueden deducirse las nuevas instalaciones a nivel cualitativo, pero cuantitativamente es más difícil, así que el instituto de análisis de IA Epoch AI ha analizado cuánta potencia de cálculo alberga y ha llegado a una conclusión: puede que sea el más grande de Huawei en China, pero está años luz del mayor datacenter del mundo, el Colossus 2 de Tennessee.
A ojo. Concretamente, su capacidad de datos es solo del 7% del de Colossus 2. O lo que es lo mismo: Colossus 2 tendría una capacidad de 14 veces más. Para 2028 Huawei está previsto que Huawei añada un nuevo edificio y crezca más de un 70%, pero Colossus 2 aumentará también.
Según Epoch AI, cuenta con cuatro edificios de refrigeración densa que alcanzan una capacidad de 286 MW, de los cuales ya están operativos tres. En su interior, habría unos 105.000 chips Ascend 910C y 8.000 Ascend 910B, equivalentes a unas 81.000 GPU Nvidia H100.
Por qué importa. Porque evidencia que el actual cuello de botella de China con los centros de datos no es la electricidad, como le pasa a Occidente, sino los chips. Según SemiAnalysis, los chips más recientes de Nvidia son unas 2,5 veces más eficientes. ¿Que significa esto? Que aunque hubiera dos centros de datos punteros, uno estadounidense y otro chino, con la misma potencia de datos, el asiático solo alcanzaría el 40% del cómputo del estadounidense.
Las malas noticias para China no terminan aquí: según Epoch aunque la distancia se reduce, esta brecha no se cerrará en esta década. Eso sí, el gigante asiático no ha dicho aún su última palabra: el campus hermano de Wuhu aspira a llegar a unos 151.000 H100e en diciembre de 2027.
El mejor fabricante y sus mejores armas. Este campus en construcción se forma parte de la iniciativa estatal "East Data West Computing" que data de 202w y que no habría sido posible sin los últimos grandes avances en materia de fabricación de chips propios (las restricciones de EEUU han servido a la vez como freno y acicate) y Huawei, su fabricante más importante. En 2025 Huawei lanzó su chip Ascend 910C que, según sus propios informes, rinde por debajo de un H100 (concretamente, equivale a un 76%). China sufre vetos, pero el desequilibrio es global: es Estados Unidos quien lleva la voz cantante del cómputo global.
Cómo lo han hecho. Para su estimación, Epoch no ha usado datos oficiales sino lo que ve desde el cielo. Así, ha contabilizado cuántas hay y ha medido su tamaño, lo que permite calcular cuánto calor pueden disipar y a partir de ahí, deducir la potencia eléctrica. Después, estima los chips a partir de las ventas de chips de Huawei considerando el desfase entre venta y despliegue, algo que ha contrastado con dos alternativas: la potencia de la subestación eléctrica (304 MW) y los generadores de respaldo (230 MW).

articles.title: 0,09 € le kilowattheure chez Auchan : Le Plein dégaine la recharge la moins chère de France pour Noël
articles.text:
Avec son tarif de 0,17 €/kWh sur ses bornes 22 kW, E.Leclerc semblait avoir décroché le titre de la recharge lente la moins chère de France. C’était sans compter sur Le Plein, qui lance avec Auchan une offre à partir de ce mardi 24 novembre 2026, faisant tomber le kilowattheure à 0,09 €. Pour en bénéficier, il faut néanmoins accepter les règles du jeu de la grande distribution.
L’enseigne et l’opérateur français n’en sont pas à leur coup d’essai. Entre le 20 juin et début septembre, Le Plein avait déjà offert la première recharge (dans la limite de 30 €), sans exiger de carte de fidélité. J’en avais d’ailleurs profité. Cette fois, la mécanique change pour les fêtes de fin d’année : pour en profiter, il faut disposer d’une carte de fidélité Waaoh! d’Auchan, et les euros gagnés se dépensent ensuite dans l’enseigne. Cela reste pour autant une bonne affaire pour recharger en temps masqué.
Un tarif imbattable, mais sous forme de cagnottage
L’offre est valable du 24 novembre au 13 janvier 2027 sur les 394 points de charge Le Plein installés sur les parkings des 23 magasins Auchan participants. Le tarif varie selon la puissance des bornes, mais toutes donnent droit à un crédit sur la carte Waaoh! :
- Recharge Éco (jusqu’à 22 kW) : 0,09 €/kWh net (0,32 € facturé, dont 0,23 € recrédités).
- Recharge Rapide (jusqu’à 100 kW) : 0,19 €/kWh net (0,42 € facturé, dont 0,23 € recrédités).
- Recharge Ultra (jusqu’à 400 kW) : 0,39 €/kWh net (0,58 € facturé, dont 0,19 € recrédités).
Prenons une recharge de 25 kWh sur une borne Rapide (jusqu’à 100 kW) : vous payez 10,50 €, mais 5,75 € sont crédités sur votre compte de fidélité Auchan, ramenant le coût de la recharge à 4,75 €. Toute la subtilité est là. L’argent ne revient pas sur votre compte bancaire mais sur votre carte de fidélité, comme chez Carrefour, qui crédite une partie de la recharge sur ses bornes lentes aux détenteurs de sa carte.
Pour en profiter, il faut impérativement posséder la carte de fidélité Waaoh!, l’associer à son compte dans l’application Le Plein, puis lancer la recharge depuis l’application ou avec la carte Le Plein. Si vous ne faites jamais vos courses chez Auchan, l’offre perd tout son intérêt puisque les euros cumulés sont à dépenser dans l’enseigne.
Une opération de notoriété avant Noël
Nous avons échangé avec Julius Dewavrin, le directeur général de Le Plein, le vendredi 20 novembre, pour en savoir plus sur l’esprit de cette offre. Il assume cette alliance avec l’ADN du distributeur pour « donner du pouvoir d’achat » et « permettre de cumuler un montant significatif pour les achats de Noël ». Il tient toutefois à rassurer sur la simplicité du dispositif : « Le tarif proposé a pour seule condition la carte Waaoh!, il n’y a pas d’abonnement. »
Derrière ce coup de pouce avant les fêtes, l’opérateur en profite aussi pour se faire connaître. Même s’il a pris la tête du classement Chargemap de l’expérience de recharge, publié en janvier 2026 à partir des avis laissés en 2025, l’opérateur reste encore méconnu en France. Jusqu’ici, la priorité était donnée au déploiement de l’infrastructure. La communication va désormais s’accélérer, mais Le Plein avance « brique par brique », selon son directeur général.
L’objectif est d’attirer les automobilistes sur ses bornes pendant le « temps masqué » des courses pour leur faire découvrir un « service simple, accessible, positif ». Si vous êtes déjà client Auchan, c’est probablement le meilleur bon plan recharge de cette fin d’année. Pour les autres, il faudra accepter de remplir son chariot au passage.
Qu’en est-il des stations Le Plein installées sur les parkings d’autres enseignes (Decathlon, Leroy Merlin, Cultura…) ? Julius Dewavrin nous a confié que l’offre Auchan ne sera pas forcément la seule à cagnottage sur laquelle Le Plein travaille pour « redonner du pouvoir d’achat aux clients », sans préciser ni l’enseigne concernée ni la date de lancement.

articles.title: Le volant de ce SUV BYD peut disparaître et c’est une première mondiale : à quoi ça sert — Frandroid
articles.text:
Il ne se passe quasiment pas un jour sans que l’on entende parler de BYD. Il faut dire que le constructeur chinois, qui emploie plus de 100 000 ingénieurs, ne cesse de lancer de nouveaux modèles sur le marché. Le groupe possède aussi plusieurs marques, dont Denza, Yangwang et Fang Cheng Bao. C’est cette dernière qui a lancé le Tai 9 en Chine, le 19 novembre 2026. Il s’agit d’un grand SUV hybride rechargeable, qui possède une petite particularité.
Le nouveau Tai 9 est, selon BYD, la première voiture de série au monde dotée d’un volant rétractable. L’idée n’est pas neuve pour autant : on l’avait notamment vue sur un concept, le Peugeot e-Legend, en 2018. Mais contrairement au concept de Peugeot, qui escamotait son volant en mode autonome, celui du Tai 9 ne se replie qu’à l’arrêt, pour des raisons évidentes de sécurité. BYD présente tout de même cette technologie comme une préparation à la conduite autonome de niveaux 3 et 4. L’opération prend 10 secondes, selon le site de la marque.
Ce tour de passe-passe n’est possible que parce que la version haut de gamme du Tai 9 n’a plus de colonne de direction : sa direction est entièrement électrique (steer-by-wire), sans lien mécanique entre le volant et les roues. Le mécanisme est conçu pour supporter 80 000 cycles, selon la marque.
Votre production solaire dépasse votre consommation ? Stockez le surplus au lieu de le revendre à bas prix. Le SolarFlow 2400 AC+ se branche sur votre installation existante, 100 % plug-and-play, et s’amortit plus vite grâce au Black Friday.
Le but de ce volant escamotable ? Augmenter le confort pour le conducteur, lorsque celui-ci attend dans le véhicule. De plus, le siège peut quant à lui s’incliner jusqu’à 165 degrés, en 20 secondes seulement.
À vrai dire, le confort est de mise dans ce grand SUV à six places (en 2+2+2), qui affiche une longueur de 5,27 mètres pour 2 mètres de large et 1,88 mètre de haut. Le tout associé à un empattement de 3,13 mètres. Un écran de 30 pouces s’étend de la console centrale jusque devant le passager, tandis qu’un autre de 21,4 pouces, accroché au plafond, équipe certaines versions pour les passagers arrière.
Plus de 300 kilomètres en électrique
Les passagers à l’arrière ont aussi droit à leur propre affichage, installé sur les sièges. Le coffre offre 655 litres, et jusqu’à 1 245 litres une fois la troisième rangée rabattue. L’habitacle cache aussi un petit frigo.
Uniquement proposé en hybride rechargeable, le nouveau Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9 s’offre un moteur thermique 1,5 litre turbo, associé à des moteurs électriques à l’avant et à l’arrière. Le tout lui permet d’atteindre une puissance maximale de 400 kW, soit 544 ch. De quoi réaliser le 0 à 100 km/h en 4,8 secondes seulement.
Le grand SUV embarque une batterie Blade, qui fait appel à la chimie LFP (lithium-fer-phosphate). Celle-ci affiche une capacité de 66,48 kWh. De quoi parcourir jusqu’à 400 kilomètres en tout électrique selon le cycle chinois CLTC, et 310 kilomètres selon le cycle WLTC, bien plus proche de la norme européenne WLTP. La recharge s’effectue de 10 à 70 % en 5 minutes, grâce à la technologie Flash Charging. Les 97 % sont atteints en seulement 9 minutes.
Toutes les versions reçoivent de série l’aide à la conduite God’s Eye B, qui fait appel à un capteur LiDAR. Ce système reste toutefois de niveau 2 : il faut garder les mains sur le volant. En Chine, le niveau 3 se limite encore à des expérimentations sur des routes désignées, avec quelques modèles de Changan et BAIC.
Le nouveau Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9 démarre à 279 900 yuans, soit environ 38 000 euros. Mais pour profiter du volant rétractable, il faut viser la finition la plus chère, facturée 329 900 yuans (environ 45 000 euros). Mais pour l’heure, il est seulement disponible dans l’Empire du Milieu.

articles.title: VC funding rebounds as startups raise $255M; Women founders driving social change
articles.text:
VC funding rebounds as startups raise $255M; Women founders driving social change
Venture capital funding in Indian startups saw a sharp rise this week, propped up by a couple of deals in the $50-million range.
Dear Reader,
India’s startup funding landscape showed signs of recovery in the third week of November, with investments jumping to $255 million from $26 million in the previous week. AI, retail, food brands and spacetech attracted investor interest, although large-ticket deals remained limited.
Meanwhile, quantum computing is beginning to show promise beyond theoretical research, with companies exploring how the technology could transform the energy sector. From optimising power grids and improving solar cell efficiency to advancing hydrogen production, quantum computers could help tackle some of the industry's most complex challenges.
However, technological advances also bring new challenges. The International Committee of the Red Cross has warned that the world is running out of time to regulate autonomous weapons as AI-powered military technologies advance rapidly. It is urging governments to agree on legally binding international rules to prevent machines from making life-and-death decisions without meaningful human control.
In other news, the global conversation on technology and sustainability continues at the policy level. COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended without consensus following disagreements over the pace of the clean-energy transition, fossil fuel commitments and climate finance for developing nations. The outcome highlights the growing challenge of balancing energy security, economic priorities and climate action.
Closer home, Meta is facing scrutiny over content moderation after the Congress party's youth wing staged protests outside its offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram over the removal of Instagram accounts belonging to party leaders. The protests have reignited concerns around online censorship, free speech and the accountability of social media platforms in India.
In today’s newsletter:
- VC funding bounces back after record low last week
- Women founders using AI to drive social change
Here’s your trivia for today: Which venture capital firm was an early investor in both Google and Amazon? (Scroll down for the answer)
Funding
VC funding bounces back after record low last week
India’s startup funding landscape showed signs of recovery in the third week of November, with investments jumping to $255 million from $26 million in the previous week. Investor interest returned across sectors, with AI, retail, food brands and spacetech attracting capital. However, the broader funding environment continues to face challenges, with large-ticket deals remaining limited.
Key takeaways:
- AI-native CRM startup Dreamteam raised $53 million, while value fashion retailer Style Union secured $52.1 million. Physical AI startup Humyn Labs followed with a $47 million round.
- Semiconductor startup Bharat Semi raised $24 million, food brand Boba Bhai secured $18 million, and robotics startup Botsync attracted $11 million.
- Only 16 deals have crossed the $100 million mark so far in 2026, pointing to continued challenges in large-scale fundraising.
Women Entrepreneurs
These women founders are using AI and emerging technologies to drive social change
From helping girls explore STEM careers to creating digital work opportunities in rural communities, women founders are finding innovative applications for emerging technologies. VigyanShaala is using its Curie Bot to encourage girls from underserved communities to pursue STEM, while Karya is enabling rural workers to earn through AI training projects that incorporate regional languages.
Key takeaways:
- Rocket Learning uses AI to support early childhood education, while Aaroogya AI Foundation applies AI to improve women's health assessments.
- BrainSightAI uses AI-powered brain imaging to help doctors understand neurological and psychiatric conditions.
- Humble Bee uses technology to help small-scale beekeepers improve hive management and productivity, while other ventures are using technology to expand access to education and healthcare.
News & updates
- Gaming Record: Grand Theft Auto VI generated a staggering $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, with publisher Rockstar Games calling it the biggest entertainment launch in history. The game sold 32.5 million units before release, while its opening-day revenue nearly quintupled the $800 million earned by its predecessor, GTA V, in 2013.
- Financial Reforms: The Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) has proposed 15 financial sector reforms to strengthen India's financial system and support its ambition of becoming a $26.5 trillion economy by 2047. Key recommendations include a permanent liquidity window for well-governed NBFCs, higher lending limits for renewable energy projects, greater foreign investment in public sector banks and improved access to credit for MSMEs.
What you should watch out for
India Analytics & AI Conference 2026 will be held on November 23 at Conrad Bengaluru, organised by the Institute of Analytics (IoA). The invitation-only event is free to attend and is expected to bring together over 200 participants.
Civo Navigate India 2026 will take place on November 24 at the Sheraton Grand Bengaluru Whitefield Hotel & Convention Center, bringing together over 1,000 technology professionals and 20+ speakers. The conference will explore developments in AI, cloud infrastructure, DevOps and data sovereignty.
Which venture capital firm was an early investor in both Google and Amazon?
Answer: Kleiner Perkins

articles.title: Après une cyberattaque, Nissan coupe un outil vital pour ses concessionnaires
articles.text:
Nissan est à nouveau dans le viseur des cybercriminels. Le constructeur automobile révèle avoir « identifié un accès non autorisé à une partie d’un système de diagnostic de véhicules utilisé par nos concessionnaires dans le monde ». Par précaution, le groupe japonais a coupé une partie de cet outil il y a dix jours, le 13 novembre. Celui-ci est toujours hors service au moment où cet article est écrit.
À lire aussi : C’est l’une des Nissan les plus populaires, mais vous ne verrez sans doute jamais sa version électrique
Des clés impossibles à reprogrammer
Le système Nissan compromis s’intitule CONSULT-III plus. Il est utilisé par les garages Nissan pour intervenir sur l’électronique des voitures et réaliser des réparations. Plusieurs fonctions en ligne ont été désactivées dans le sillage de la cyberattaque, à savoir la programmation des calculateurs de la voiture, le déverrouillage de certains modules et la gestion de l’antidémarrage, le système antivol électronique présent dans toutes les voitures récentes, qui empêche le moteur de démarrer si la clé n’est pas reconnue.
Concrètement, un client qui a perdu ou abîmé sa clé ne peut pas en faire programmer une nouvelle chez son concessionnaire. Selon les informations du New York Times, certaines réparations électroniques peuvent aussi être retardées.
En dépit de l’attaque informatique, les concessions Nissan restent ouvertes et peuvent effectuer la plupart des autres interventions, rassure le groupe nippon. L’entreprise précise que la nouvelle version de l’outil, baptisée CONSULT-IV, n’a pas été touchée par la cyberattaque. Sur son site destiné aux professionnels, Nissan indique que la coupure a été prolongée le temps de terminer l’enquête, sans donner de date de retour à la normale. Pour le moment, on ignore encore qui est derrière l’attaque, depuis quand les pirates avaient accès au système et si des données de clients ont été volées durant l’opération.
À lire aussi : Nissan va avoir un système de conduite autonome similaire à Tesla
Nissan, une cible récurrente pour les pirates
Ce n’est pas la première fois que Nissan se retrouve dans le viseur des hackers. En 2017, le fabricant automobile s’est déjà retrouvé dans le viseur du ransomware WannaCry. Plus récemment, c’est le gang Red Hat qui a piraté l’un des prestataires de Nissan, compromettant les données de plus de 20 000 clients.

articles.title: Meta lanzó una extensión de Chrome para que su agente de IA Muse navegue con la cuenta del usuario
articles.text:
Meta publicó una extensión de Chrome que instala a su agente de IA Muse, un asistente que ejecuta tareas por su cuenta, en el panel lateral del navegador de Google. Alexandr Wang, director de IA de Meta, informó en X que 200.000 personas ya la usan.
La extensión, llamada “Muse from Meta”, figura en la tienda oficial de Chrome con una calificación de 4,5 sobre 5 en 257 valoraciones. Funciona en Chrome 137 o posterior y se abre con el atajo Alt+Shift+C. Para usarla hace falta una cuenta de Muse.
Según la ficha de la tienda, Muse puede completar formularios, comparar precios, hacer reservas y hacer seguimiento de reembolsos sin que el usuario salga de la página que tiene abierta. También puede conectarse con el correo, el calendario, Instagram, Facebook y datos de salud y finanzas.
Wang escribió que el aviso era “tardío”: la extensión ya estaba disponible desde antes. El sitio TestingCatalog la detectó el 13 de noviembre, cuando Meta todavía no había dicho nada.
Qué puede hacer Muse dentro del navegador personal
Muse navega con el Chrome del propio usuario. Abre sus pestañas en un grupo aparte y solo puede actuar dentro de ellas, según la página de ayuda de Meta. La empresa afirma que el agente no ve las contraseñas guardadas, el historial de navegación ni la configuración del navegador, y que las claves que aparecen en una página se eliminan del texto antes de que Muse lo lea.
La misma página de ayuda aclara un límite: Muse puede usar cualquier sitio en el que la persona ya haya iniciado sesión, sin pedirle de nuevo sus datos de acceso. Por eso Meta recomienda cerrar sesión en las cuentas que el usuario no quiera que el agente utilice, antes de conectar la extensión.
Meta también advierte que los sitios web y el navegador pueden registrar información a partir de la actividad de Muse y atribuirla al usuario. Esa actividad puede aparecer en su cuenta de Google y en su historial, y puede afectar los anuncios, las recomendaciones y los contenidos que ve dentro y fuera de los productos de Meta.
La ficha de Chrome Web Store declara que la extensión maneja información personal identificable, datos de salud, información financiera y de pago, datos de autenticación, comunicaciones personales, ubicación e historial web. El desarrollador indica que esos datos no se venden a terceros, salvo en los usos aprobados.
Los controles que ofrece Meta
Meta afirma que el usuario puede aprobar acciones antes de que ocurran, revisar un registro completo de actividad y revocar cualquier conexión cuando quiera. Para frenar al agente basta con hacer clic en la página, presionar Esc o sacar la pestaña del grupo de Muse. La extensión también puede desinstalarse desde la configuración de Chrome.
La empresa reconoce que Muse puede cometer errores o tomar acciones inesperadas, y pide al usuario que supervise su trabajo.
Un antecedente de fallas recientes
El lanzamiento llega pocos días después de una investigación de Reuters, publicada el 18 de noviembre, basada en más de dos docenas de mensajes internos de empleados de Meta. Los textos describían acciones de Muse que nadie había pedido, entre ellas un recordatorio sobre un mensaje de Signal que la empleada no había conectado al agente.
Reuters probó con personal de Signal y del AI Now Institute, una organización sin fines de lucro que estudia el impacto social de la IA, y replicó ese acceso en un teléfono Android y en una computadora Apple. Un vocero de Meta, Daniel Roberts, calificó los ejemplos de “incidentes aislados” y dijo que Muse accede a otras aplicaciones solo con permisos que el usuario concede de forma explícita.
Según The Next Web, Muse suma 10 millones de usuarios desde su lanzamiento en septiembre y llegó a Australia el martes 18 de noviembre. Meta no ha informado una fecha para nuevos países en el caso de la extensión; los medios leídos no precisan en qué mercados está disponible, más allá de que no funciona en Emiratos Árabes Unidos ni en Arabia Saudita, según el sitio tbreak.

articles.title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections. And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power.
In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”
“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”
He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”
During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.
I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?
Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.
I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.
Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.
Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.
It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.
Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?
I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago, where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.
And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity, and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.
And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant.
That was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention.
You don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now.
Absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable.
They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed.
I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies, but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do.
And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious with generative AI and the data centers to power them, where many of the benefits that were supposed to come of generative AI do not appear to have materialized — whether those are the economic benefits, the productivity benefits, but also the the benefits of delivery of services like healthcare and education to the public, as we heard Sam Altman saying a lot in the in the early days of ChatGPT.
Paired with that, there has been this massive environmental cost […] but there’s also this massive and growing social cost, when you think about the mental health impacts of chatbot dependence, of all the false information that pervades social media platforms now, of the deepfake crisis, and I could go on and on and on.
It’s not surprising that there has been backlash. But I have been surprised at how widespread it’s been, and also how bipartisan — you talk about Ron DeSantis and Bernie Sanders both being opposed to data centers. Why do you think it’s become such a unifying issue?
Because it’s not an abstract issue, right? I think even when we think about generative AI or social media or something like that, [it] can feel abstract. It’s a service that you access from your phone or from your computer. It’s not something that is tangible in the world.
But when a data center is coming to set up shop in your community, it’s very physical, it’s very material. It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on. You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.
I think that there was already a pre-existing frustration with the tech industry that came from the quality of the products, the effects that they’re having on our society and our lives. For some people, [they have] frustration with the way that the tech industry has been collaborating with the Trump administration and with right-wing political groups in different parts of the world. But then you add on top of that the actual effects that come of having one of these infrastructures be planned or located in your community, and that anger gets kind of directed into that physical manifestation of this thing that you have an issue with.
Obviously, the data centers are at the forefront of this, and it’s what we pay the most attention to. But we also see this increasingly with other aspects of the tech industry, whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.
There’s a lot of frustration with the physical manifestations of the tech industry, because that is something that can really be felt more directly, but can also be challenged more directly. You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? It doesn’t often seem like very much.
The tech companies have reacted to this backlash in a few different ways. One is that Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI have all talked about [their commitment] that they’re not going to use NDAs anymore in their negotiations with local governments. How big a difference do you think that will make?
Not a huge difference.
I do think it’s going to be good that it will be easier for people to access information on these projects that are being located in their communities. But part of the reason why we’re seeing these shifts is exactly in response to that opposition.
We’re seeing the tech companies propose to pay for more of the electricity infrastructure that will be required for their data centers to reduce the pressure on ratepayers, because people are angry about that. They’re promising to use different water-based cooling systems in their data centers, to say that they’re able to use less electricity.
When we look at the NDAs and the decision or the announcement that they’re not going to use those anymore, I think it’s also because it’s working against them. People know what a data center is now, and if people find out that a data center is coming to town and they have questions and they’re not getting answers, that’s only going to further fuel the opposition to those data centers.
So, it’s not really a surprise to see [the tech companies] do this, and it’s a way that they can get a positive PR thing by saying, “We’re not going to use these NDAs that are working against us anyway. “
One of the other ways they’ve responded is by saying that there’s a lot of misinformation about the environmental harms, or that they’re being overstated, or that they can mitigate them with renewable technology. How valid do you think those arguments are?
I think that the industry recognizes that there is a lot of concern and they’re trying to basically move into the discussion with narratives of their own to have people question whether data centers are really a problem or not.
I feel like we don’t see the industry doing as much on the energy side anymore, particularly on the fossil fuel side, because they realize that they have kind of lost that argument. If you look back a year and a half, two years ago, they were talking a lot about renewables, about nuclear energy, you don’t hear so much of that discourse anymore.
They have pivoted, instead, to focus on the water question, where I think that they feel that they can use more abstract national figures in order to confuse the public about what’s going on. They can say, “If you look nationally, agriculture and golf courses also use a lot of water. So you don’t need to be worried about a data center coming to tow,n because they don’t use as much, in aggregate.”
But the issue with data center water use is not a national issue. It’s a local issue. There are unquestionably going to be communities where they seek to locate data centers that are going to have plenty of water and that are not going to be concerned about a data center coming to town. But they’re also locating [data centers] in a lot of communities that are experiencing high degrees of water stress, which means that they don’t have the water to really provide to these infrastructures.
We have also seen them pivoting to move away from the evaporative cooling systems, the ones that require a lot of water — because you need to take in a certain amount of water as it gets too hot, it evaporates away, and so you can see why you need a consistent flow of water into the data center for that type of cooling system — to a closed loop system, where you basically have a certain amount of water, it stays within the data center, you keep cooling it down by using electricity to do that, and so you clearly don’t need as much water.
That is their new way to say, “Hey, don’t worry about the water use. We’re going to switch to this other system.” But the issue there, of course, is that it does require more electricity in order to keep that water cooled down, and that is often not part of what they talk about or discuss when they are proposing that as an alternative.
Then the other thing is that it’s not just water that is in those pipes or tubes going through the data center. There’s also a lot of coolant in there, a lot of chemicals, and communities where these projects are being located with closed loop cooling systems are becoming increasingly concerned about those coolants leaking out into their water supply and what that is going to mean.
In the book, you say repeatedly that you’re not against technology itself or even data centers in general, but [against] this hyperscale approach. The book is called “Hyperscale.” The last chapter is called “Human Scale.” Why do you see scale as such an important part of the problem?
Because scale is what creates the pressures, whether those are the pressures on the communities or you know the pressures on our wider electricity system and whatnot.
I don’t think that the inherent problem is data centers, because we have had data centers for a long time, and sure, there have been occasional concerns about specific projects, but data centers as a whole have not been an issue that the public has felt merited this degree of attention. So that is why I feel the hyperscale data center, and particularly the acceleration that we’ve seen in the expansion of the size of these hyperscale data centers, but also the number of data centers that these companies are building out, is notable in this moment.
Linked to that is not just the scale of the demand created by these hyperscale data centers, but also, what they are supposed to be powering? That is where the other disconnect lies. They’re demanding a lot, but if we were actually getting something good for it, this might be justified. I think that for a lot of people, and I feel like we see this reflected in polling, they’re not actually seeing the benefits from generative AI.
So then the question becomes: “Okay, we’re expending all of these resources, we’re pushing up emissions such that climate change is going to be accelerated just to build out all these data centers to meet the ambitions of generative AI that the tech companies have, but then we’re not actually getting much benefit out of that technology. So what are we actually doing here?”
One other thing that really struck a chord with me was your description about how tech executives often talk about the future as if there’s [just one] inevitable future. The only thing that’s in question is how quickly we arrive there [and] who’s going to make the most money off of it.
This is so important for me, because I do feel like how we think about the future then shapes decisions that we make. The tech billionaires, they see the future in a certain way […] and I think that they have been very successful in getting us to buy into their vision of the future for the past several decades. But that does not mean that that is the only way that the future has to be.
We can imagine a very different kind of future, and that would mean that we place our resources in different places and actually develop technology in a different way, toward different outcomes, with different incentives driving that work.
There are interesting conversations happening in different parts of the world right now around things like digital sovereignty, getting off of these technologies from the U.S. tech companies. But in some cases, those conversations are quickly captured by industry in those different parts of the world to say, “Okay, we want to get off U.S. technology, but let’s have our local companies do effectively the same thing, and just let them do the same exploitative practices and make the money that the U.S. tech companies would be making.” And I don’t think that that is the right way forward.
I also think that there is a role for public sector development of technology in a way that we’ve eschewed or even looked at skeptically for the past number of decades, because the idea was that technology had to be left to the private sector. What we’re starting to see in Europe is a bit more funding of public technology, in order to develop the services that government itself depends on, and I think that that is a good first step.
But especially when we’re looking at the Microsoft outage that happened just recently, and we’re looking at Google threatening schools with their access to Google search if they don’t accept Google AI tool, I think that there’s a real moment right now to put resources into developing something different, that doesn’t come from these major tech companies, and that hopefully can have much more public benefit than what these companies now provide us.

articles.title: TSMC reportedly pauses shipments to Chinese designers after U.S. export rules flag decade-old 16nm and 14nm nodes — new BIS controls threaten smartphone, TV, and automotive chips
articles.text:
TSMC reportedly pauses shipments to Chinese designers after U.S. export rules flag decade-old 16nm and 14nm nodes — new BIS controls threaten smartphone, TV, and automotive chips
Chips designers have to prove that their semiconductors do not break U.S. export control rules.
The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has released an interim final rule (IFR) [PDF] that will prevent Chinese AI companies from leasing data compute outside of China to access advanced U.S. chips like Nvidia Blackwell AI GPUs. However, Nikkei Asia reports that the new regulations have also affected foundries making chips for consumers and the automotive industry, as TSMC has put several shipments to both Chinese and non-Chinese chip designers on hold as it reviews their compliance with the changes to U.S.
Washington’s previous export controls only focused on high-performance AI chips like Nvidia’s Blackwell and upcoming Vera Rubin chips. The new rules expand it to include all chips, with front-end fabricators (chip foundries) or OSATs (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test companies), also known as packaging and testing companies, required to assume that semiconductors with a 16nm or 14nm node are automatically classified as export-controlled advanced computing chips. The ruling even mentioned that even if the designed chip has less than 30 billion transistors and has no HBM, it cannot be assumed that the chips aren’t built for high-performance computing.
The 16nm and 14nm nodes have been around for around 10 years now, and they could even be found inside consumer devices like smartphones and TVs, as well as in automotive applications. This new rule means that designers making chips using 16nm or newer nodes, even if they’re not specifically built for data centers, must secure documentation from an approved designer certifying the chip’s Total Processing Performance or performance density if they want to avoid additional scrutiny from the fab.
"The new rule is very strict this time, and the affecting scope is far beyond only chips for data centers but covers smartphone processors, autonomous driving and other types of chips for consumer electronics as well as others if they are using nodes that are 14nm or 16nm or more advanced tech," a source told the publication. "The move would delay shipments to many chip developers worldwide before they can clear compliance and hit many emerging startups in many Asian nations."
Aside from this, the U.S. also now requires export licenses to ship advanced AI chips to the following countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil, and Thailand. The IFR says that these countries are often used as transshipment points for chips that are being diverted to China, as evidenced by the Supermicro and Megaspeed investigations, which used one of these countries as the destination of the Nvidia servers they ordered, before sending them forward to their final destination in China.
Chip smuggling has long been a simmering issue in the United States, but it seemingly has bubbled over after the revelation of Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who’s also suspected of being instrumental in diverting $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips and passing on information to Chinese intelligence. While his alleged relationship with a direct subordinate was the apparent primary cause of his departure from Nvidia, sources say that the real reason behind his ousting is the mass smuggling of 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs that happened right under his nose.

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: A/B testing robots vs. humans | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.
There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?
A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.
Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.
A/B test: humans vs. robots
A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.
Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.
Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.
Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.)
That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.
It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.
A little bird
You might have seen the Wall Street Journal scoop that General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible candidates to replace CEO Mary Barra. Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes.
I reached out to a few little birds to learn more and here’s what they’re telling me. And, for the record, GM declined to comment.
GM has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, according to one source, who noted it’s possible that the board has other executive search firms working on this as well. The board is taking a two-track approach to its search, which is occurring simultaneously.
The first is focused on traditional yet transformative automotive CEOs. One name that has come up from the executive search firm is José Muñoz, who is president and CEO of Hyundai. The board is also interested in someone less traditional. The firm has apparently floated names like Doug Field, who recently became CEO of Mind Robotics, and Larry Culp of GE, according to a source with direct information.
There are internal GM folks who are also in the mix, including Sterling Anderson, co-founder of self-driving trucks company Aurora who became chief product officer at GM in May 2025, and Paul Jacobson, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.
Got a tip for us? Email Kirsten Korosec at [email protected].
Deals!
Elysian Aircraft, the Dutch aerospace company developing aviation electrification technologies, raised €12 million in private and public funding from FideFlux, SecFund, and ROM InWest, as well as from individual investors and family offices.
Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, an electric three-wheeler business under Mahindra & Mahindra, is looking at an IPO in about 18 months, per Bloomberg.
Numa, a startup developing an AI operating system for dealerships, raised a $45 million Series C round led by New York-based Blue Cloud Ventures. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, and Tokio Marine Future Fund also participated.
Stark Future, a European electric motorcycle company, raised at least €150 million in equity, Reuters reported. The raise was led by Highland Europe, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s 1GT and Axon Partners Group.
Vincue, an automotive tech company that sells software to dealerships, raised $93 million in a round led by Wavecrest Growth Partners, with continued backing from FM Capital.
Notable reads and other tidbits
Also, the electric micromobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has paused deliveries of its new e-bike over problems with its software and batteries, The Verge reported.
Edmunds released new data that found the average new vehicle is selling for a record $50,087.
Redwood Materials is using computer vision and machine learning to identify and sort batteries by chemistry before they’re fed into the company’s rotary calciner — a massive cylindrical industrial furnace used to process 40,000 metric tons of raw feedstock a year.
Tesla said it will spend about $3.3 billion to expand its Berlin gigafactory to produce Cybercabs — yet another signal of the company’s global autonomy ambitions.
Over the weekend, Tesla invited “select customers” to preorder the company’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.” The Cybercab is priced at $29,990, but there is a lot more to ownership. The company will charge owners $299 a month to use the vehicles, delivery will only occur in a handful of cities, and operations will be limited to specific locations.
Uber opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities. Uber already has a service for teenagers. If this program proves successful, it would open Uber up to another market of customers: busy families.
Meanwhile, Uber said it’s notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in an October data breach.
Zipline continues to scale its autonomous drone delivery business, this time in its partnership with Uber. The companies had previously announced a partnership for drones to deliver for Uber Eats, but it officially launched this week in a Houston suburb. The aim is a big one: Uber and Zipline say they aim to make 1 million deliveries a day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.
One more thing …
I had a chance to catch up with (and interview) Ro Gupta, the head of Woven Capital — Toyota’s growth fund.
I’ve known Gupta for years; we first met when I worked at Fortune and he had a startup called Carmera. A lot has happened since those AV 1.0 days, and Gupta caught us up on this next era of AV innovation and where Toyota is interested in investing. It’s not enough to simply state “AI.” There’s more to it than that. Take a listen.

articles.title: Zhipu lance GLM-5.4 pour les développeurs : vision, contexte d’un million de tokens et architecture « en boucle » inédite — Frandroid
articles.text:
Pas d’article de blog, pas de tableau de benchmarks, pas de fichier à télécharger : GLM-5.4 est apparu dans un menu déroulant. Les abonnés du GLM Coding Plan l’ont découvert en ouvrant leur sélecteur de modèles, accompagné de deux étiquettes, « vision » et « 1M ».
Pour une entreprise qui s’est fait un nom en publiant ses modèles en accès libre, le lancement est étonnamment feutré. Il s’agit pourtant, selon Caixin, du premier grand modèle chinois bâti sur une architecture « en boucle », que l’équipe dit avoir poussée pendant trois mois.
Derrière Z.ai, on trouve Zhipu AI, une société pékinoise née à l’université Tsinghua. C’est la première grande entreprise chinoise de modèles de langage à être entrée en Bourse, à Hong Kong en janvier 2026, et elle figure depuis janvier 2025 sur la liste noire commerciale américaine (Entity List), qui lui ferme l’accès à certaines technologies made in USA. GLM-5.4 succède à GLM-5.3, sorti à la mi-août, dont les poids (les fichiers qui permettent de faire tourner le modèle sur ses propres serveurs) ont été publiés deux semaines plus tard sur Hugging Face, après une revue de sécurité.
La disponibilité a été annoncée sur X par Zixuan Li, responsable de l’écosystème international de Z.ai, puis par le compte officiel de l’entreprise. La nouveauté la plus visible comble un vrai trou : GLM-5.3 ne lisait que du texte, alors que GLM-5.4 accepte images et vidéos. On peut lui montrer la capture d’une interface cassée au lieu de la décrire en trois paragraphes.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
Une boucle dans le Transformer, et pas grand-chose d’autre
Mais il y a aussi une nouveauté technique assez intéressante : Loop Transformer. C’est ce qu’on appelle une architecture en boucle en bon français. Et ça s’explique assez simplement.
Un modèle classique fait passer chaque token (un morceau de mot) une seule fois à travers sa pile de couches de calcul. Une architecture en boucle repasse plusieurs fois par le même bloc de couches avant de répondre, ce qui donne au modèle plus de « profondeur de réflexion » sans multiplier sa taille, puisque ce sont les mêmes paramètres qui resservent.
L’équipe de Zhipu parle d’ailleurs de « la surprise apportée par le Loop Transformer ». Elle n’a publié ni le nombre de boucles, ni la taille du modèle, ni la moindre fiche technique. Morgan Stanley évoque plus de 700 milliards de paramètres, un chiffre que l’entreprise n’a pas confirmé.
Côté performances, c’est le désert officiel. Le seul chiffre indépendant vient de KingBench 4, un banc d’essai de programmation tenu par un seul développeur : GLM-5.4 y obtient 33,2 sur 60, soit 5,7 points de plus que GLM-5.3, mais seulement la septième place sur 19, loin derrière Claude Fable 5.2 (42).
Pour situer l’enjeu, l’indice d’Artificial Analysis, qui agrège une dizaine de tests et sert de référence dans le secteur, place le meilleur modèle ouvert actuel, Kimi K3.1 Pro de Moonshot AI, à 12 points du leader propriétaire. GLM-5.4 n’y est pas encore classé.
Quant au caractère « ouvert », il reste théorique : aucun poids publié, aucune licence annoncée. Et GLM-5.3 a déjà abandonné la licence MIT au profit d’une licence maison, qui impose une revue de sécurité aux hébergeurs réalisant plus de 10 milliards de dollars de chiffre d’affaires.
Comment l’essayer dès maintenant
Pour l’instant, GLM-5.4 est réservé aux abonnés du GLM Coding Plan, la formule de Z.ai pensée pour les assistants de programmation, facturée à partir de 18 dollars par mois (prix américain, hors taxes). Pas d’accès à l’API à l’usage, pas de tarif au token, rien sur OpenRouter.
Dans Claude Code, l’agent de programmation d’Anthropic qu’on peut rediriger vers les serveurs de Z.ai, on règle le modèle sur « glm-5.4[1m] » pour profiter du million de tokens.
Dans OpenCode et les outils similaires, « glm-5.4 » suffit, et dans Z Code, l’éditeur maison, il faut ajouter l’identifiant à la main. Les formules à quota hebdomadaire offrent 50 % d’utilisation en plus qu’avec GLM-5.3, une façon assez habile de pousser tout le monde vers le nouveau modèle.
Enfin, GLM-5.5 est déjà prévu pour décembre avec quelque 3 000 milliards de paramètres, selon Caixin.

articles.title: CII proposes 15 financial sector reforms to boost long-term growth ambitions
articles.text:
CII proposes 15 financial sector reforms to boost long-term growth ambitions
Industry body CII has proposed 15 financial sector reforms, including a permanent liquidity window for well-governed NBFCs and higher priority sector lending limits for renewable energy.
In a bid to strengthen India's financial system for long-term growth ambitions, the industry body CII has proposed 15 financial sector reforms, including a permanent liquidity window for well-governed NBFCs and higher priority sector lending limits for renewable energy.
The recommendations come against the backdrop of the government's constitution of a High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat, announced in the Union Budget 2026-27.
The Committee has a six-month mandate to examine the long-term capital requirements of banks, development finance institutions, and NBFCs; review priority sector lending norms; prepare a roadmap for AI and digital adoption; and examine prudential regulations.
CII Director General Chandrajit Banerjee noted that the financial sector enters this phase from a position of strength, with healthy bank and NBFC balance sheets and a series of important measures by the government and regulators over the past year.
"The task now is to build a system that can finance an economy several times its present size by 2047. That requires deeper and longer-tenor pools of capital, credit that reaches the sectors that will drive growth, and regulation that keeps pace with how finance is delivered. Our recommendations are intended to take the current reform effort to its next stage," Banerjee said.
CII estimates that a $26.5 trillion economy by 2047 would require financial assets of nearly $106 trillion, compared with around $7 trillion at present. It said banking assets would need to grow 3-3.5 percentage points faster than nominal GDP.
The industry body also flagged the relatively shallow corporate bond market, which accounts for around 15 per cent of GDP in India, compared with 36 per cent in China and over 80 per cent in South Korea.
To advance the ongoing reform push to its next phase, CII has called for raising the priority sector lending limit for renewable energy projects from Rs 35 crore to Rs 80-100 crore per borrower and including circular economy activities such as recycling and battery reuse within the framework.
For NBFCs, CII has sought a permanent, rule-based liquidity and refinance window for well-governed entities, with access linked to compliance status, collateral standards and eligibility criteria.
It has also sought to reduce the threshold for NBFCs under the SARFAESI Act from Rs 20 lakh to Rs 1 lakh, bringing them on par with banks and housing finance companies.
Other proposals include access to Debt Recovery Tribunals, the Central Repository of Information on Large Credits and central fraud registries, subject to appropriate safeguards and reciprocal data-sharing obligations.
To deepen corporate bond markets, CII has recommended allowing pension funds, insurers and provident funds calibrated exposure to bonds rated below AA and longer-tenor instruments.
In the insurance sector, the industry body has called for restoring input tax credit for individual health and life insurance policies by making them zero-rated rather than exempt under GST.
Other recommendations include raising the voting rights cap in private banks from 26 per cent to up to 49 per cent with governance safeguards, and increasing the foreign investment limit in public sector banks from 20 per cent to 49 per cent to help them raise capital.
CII has also called for extending the Account Aggregator framework to public databases, including land records, eMandi transactions, NREGA records and ration card data, subject to consent safeguards.
For MSMEs, CII has recommended making insurance cover against risks such as fire, floods, machinery breakdown and business interruption a standard feature of government-guaranteed loans. It estimates the MSME credit gap at Rs 25-30 lakh crore.
The remaining proposals include rationalising investment limits for insurers and pension funds, finalising the climate finance taxonomy, improving regulatory predictability for NBFCs, deepening domestic institutional capital for private equity and venture capital, and permitting certified automated video-based KYC.

articles.title: En 1961, unos niños imitaron a un adulto que pegaba a un muñeco. Unos ratones de Princeton han empezado a explicar por qué
articles.text:
En 1961, en la guardería de la Universidad de Stanford, Albert Bandura reunió a 72 niños de tres a cinco años y los sentó delante de un adulto. Acto seguido, el adulto la tomó con un muñeco hinchable: lo tumbó, le pegó con un mazo en la cabeza e, incluso, lo lanzó por los aires. Luego Bandura dejó a cada niño a solas con el muñeco. Muchos repetían la paliza casi golpe por golpe.
Aquel experimento es la base de sesenta y cinco años de literatura sobre aprendizaje por observación. Sin embargo, del mecanismo psiconeuronal hemos sabido muy poco. Nadie podía mirar dentro de la cabeza de esos niños y no teníamos tecnología para hacerlo de otra manera.
Ahora, un laboratorio del Princeton Neuroscience Institute ha dado con la forma de hacerlo con ratones y, de premio, ha visto cómo se reajusta el circuito que está detrás de este tipo de aprendizajes. Es decir, el circuito vicario de la violencia.
¿Qué hicieron? El equipo de Princeton (liderado por Annegret Falkner) montó algo parecido a un gimnasio de boxeo para ratones. Durante ocho días, a tres sesiones de diez minutos al día, diez machos practicaron contra un rival sumiso y fácil de batir. Organizaron un buen puñado de peleas sin riesgo que otros siete ratones estaban mirando desde un altillo. Como grupo control, hubo seis ratones más jugando con muñecos.
Al noveno día, los tres grupos de ratones pasaron la misma prueba: tres interacciones de cuatro minutos con un macho de su tamaño, con experiencia y seleccionado a propósito por su agresividad.
Lo que no cambió. Esto quizás sea una de las cosas más curiosas: ocho días de entrenamiento, ya fuera pegando o mirando, no hicieron que esos ratones 'pegaran más' que el resto. Sí cambiaron la forma en la que lo hacían y, como consecuencia, recibieron menos golpes. No es raro porque los ratones del grupo control hicieron lo propio de un animal estresado: intentar huir y pasar más tiempo de espaldas ante el agresor.
¿Y cómo pudieron ver dentro del cráneo? Porque, hasta ahora, el experimento nos permite asociar ver la pelea con el cambio de conducta, pero no hay nada sobre los mecanismos neuronales subyacentes. Para ello, el equipo de Falkner pasó un año afinando un implante de doce fibras ópticas capaz de registrar a la vez doce nodos subcorticales de la red del comportamiento social (el hipotálamo ventromedial ventrolateral o VMHvl, la amígdala medial, el septum lateral ventral y nueve más) y la liberación de dopamina en el núcleo accumbens. Esa es la pieza técnica clave y la que permite ver en toda la red lo que antes solo se había visto en una región.
Descubrieron que ver un ataque enciende casi toda la red. De hecho, fue especialmente activa en las zonas conocidas por tener un papel inhibitorio de la agresión. Los controles no sufrieron esa activación. Además, por si fuera poco, los espectadores aprendían tanto del agresor como del agredido.
¿En qué se traduce todo esto? En que el aprendizaje vicario de la agresión afloja los frenos. El mecanismo quedó bien identificado. Hasta el punto de que los investigadores diseñaron un procedimiento que devolvía esa inhibición y, al aplicarlo, los animales que vieron la pelea se comportaban como el grupo control.
Lo interesante (y un poco agridulce) es que para que esos mecanismos se activen hace falta ver una pelea de verdad. Las peleas simuladas (con muñecos u objetos similares) no mostraron esa activación ni ese aprendizaje. Y no deja de ser curioso porque esta aventura científica empezó precisamente con un muñeco (aunque, probablemente, los niños de tres a cinco años no entendieron nunca bien la diferencia).
